column2: Platform operations"Your SOC team has identified that multiple playbooks across different environments contain identical user notification and approval workflows. You want to centralize this workflow to improve maintenance efficiency and ensure that updates automatically propagate to all playbooks using this logic. What should you do?
column3: Use environment groups to share a single playbook across multiple environments with environment-specific variable substitution.
column4: Create a master playbook template and use the duplicate function to copy it to all environments when updates are needed.
column5: Create a playbook block with input parameters for customization and output values, then insert the block into parent playbooks.
column6: Configure scheduled jobs that periodically sync playbook configurations across all environments using the SOAR API.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that let you implement common workflows across multiple playbooks. Any edit to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it. Blocks support input parameters for customization and can return output values to the parent playbook for conditional logic. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Data management"You are creating a Cloud Logging sink to export VPC Flow Logs to BigQuery for network security analysis. After creating the sink, you receive an error indicating that log entries cannot be written to the BigQuery dataset. You have verified that the dataset exists and is not a linked dataset. What is the most likely cause and resolution for this error?
column3: The sink filter syntax is invalid for VPC Flow Logs, causing the sink to reject all matching log entries. Update the filter to use the correct log name format.
column4: The sink's writer identity service account does not have the BigQuery Data Editor role on the destination dataset. Grant the BigQuery Data Editor role to the service account.
column5: The BigQuery dataset location does not match the Cloud Logging region where the logs originate. Create a new dataset in the matching region.
column6: The BigQuery dataset is configured with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) that are incompatible with Cloud Logging. Disable CMEK on the dataset.
column8: When creating a sink to route logs to BigQuery, Logging creates a service account (writer identity) that requires the BigQuery Data Editor role to write log entries to the dataset. Without this permission, the sink cannot route logs to BigQuery. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2

column2: Your organization recently activated Security Command Center Premium and wants to leverage asset discovery capabilities. You discover that the Security Command Center API asset methods are deprecated. What is the recommended approach to view and query assets in Security Command Center?
column3: Configure a third-party Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) tool to discover and catalog assets independently of Security Command Center.
column4: Use Cloud Asset Inventory to query and manage assets, as SCC now uses Cloud Asset Inventory for asset discovery which operates automatically.
column5: Enable asset discovery in the Security Command Center organization settings and continue using the Security Command Center API for asset queries.
column6: Deploy the SCC discovery client CLI on each project to scan and inventory assets, then aggregate results in a central database.
column8: Security Command Center asset management operations have been migrated to Cloud Asset Inventory. Cloud Asset Inventory discovers assets automatically and serves as the source of asset data for Security Command Center. Organizations should use Cloud Asset Inventory APIs and tools for comprehensive asset management. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-configure-asset-discovery

column2: Your organization recently enabled Security Command Center Premium tier. After one week, Security Health Analytics generates hundreds of findings daily, many of which are related to non-production environments where strict security controls are not required. You want to reduce alert fatigue for your security team while ensuring findings are still available for audit purposes. What should you do?
column3: Configure continuous exports to Pub/Sub with filters that exclude non-production findings from being sent to your notification system.
column4: Delete the non-production findings manually on a weekly basis to keep the findings list manageable.
column5: Create dynamic mute rules with filters that specify the non-production projects or folders to automatically mute current and future findings for those environments.
column6: Disable Security Health Analytics detectors for the non-production projects to stop generating findings entirely.
column8: Dynamic mute rules automatically mute findings matching your filter criteria while keeping them available for audit and compliance purposes. Muted findings are hidden by default but can be viewed by adding mute='MUTED' to queries, maintaining audit trails while reducing analyst workload. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your security team needs to write a YARA-L detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) that triggers when a user performs sensitive actions while having an elevated risk score from established behavioral baselines. The rule must incorporate entity risk scores from the Risk Analytics feature. What is the correct approach to retrieve and use entity risk scores in a YARA-L rule?
column3: Join an entity with a UDM event using the graph source qualifier and specify a risk window size of either 86400 seconds (24 hours) or 604800 seconds (7 days) in the rule.
column4: Create an entity-only rule using the ENTITY_RISK_CHANGE event type without specifying any risk window parameters in the rule definition.
column5: Configure custom risk score thresholds in the Settings page and reference those thresholds using reference lists in the YARA-L rule events section.
column6: Query the entity context directly using the udm source qualifier and calculate risk scores dynamically within the outcome section of the rule.
column8: According to Google SecOps documentation, to retrieve an entity risk score you must join an entity with a UDM event and retrieve the specified field from EntityRisk. The only supported risk windows are 24 hours (86,400 seconds) or 7 days (604,800 seconds). Using inconsistent windows or omitting the risk window size leads to inaccurate results. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-entity-risk-score

column2: You are developing a threat hunting hypothesis in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to identify anomalous behavior by privileged users. You need to correlate user login events with entity context from Active Directory to identify when administrator accounts access systems outside their normal working hours. Which approach enables this context-aware detection?
column3: Create a single-event detection rule that checks the principal.user.attribute.roles field within individual login events to identify administrator logins.
column4: Use UDM Search to filter login events by timestamp and manually cross-reference each user against the Active Directory organizational unit export.
column5: Export login events to BigQuery and join them with a manually uploaded Active Directory table to identify administrator accounts.
column6: Create a YARA-L rule that joins UDM login events with entity context from the entity graph using a shared user identifier and filters on the ADMINISTRATOR role type.
column8: Google SecOps enriches entities with context from sources like Active Directory and stores this in the entity graph. Detection rules can join UDM events with entity context using the graph namespace to access attributes like user roles, enabling context-aware detections that consider organizational hierarchy and permissions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/context-aware-analytics

column2: You are planning to implement Event Threat Detection custom modules for your enterprise and need to understand the service limits. Your organization plans to create custom modules for detecting connections to multiple threat intelligence feeds with different IP address lists. What is the default quota limit for creating custom modules per organization?
column3: 500 custom modules per organization
column4: 100 custom modules per organization
column5: 200 custom modules per organization
column6: 50 custom modules per organization
column8: The default quota limit for creating Event Threat Detection custom modules is 200 per organization. Additionally, each custom module has a size limit of 6 MB, and there is a limit of 200 custom module findings per parent resource (organization or project) per hour. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium and wants to implement automated remediation for security findings using Cloud Run functions. The function needs to modify IAM policies on affected resources when specific vulnerability findings are detected. Which IAM configuration follows the principle of least privilege for the Cloud Run function's service account?
column3: Configure the Cloud Run function to use the Security Command Center service agent account since it already has access to findings and resources being monitored.
column4: Assign the roles/securitycenter.admin role to the Cloud Run function service account so it can access all SCC findings and remediate any detected security issues.
column5: Use the Compute Engine default service account with roles/editor assigned at the organization level to ensure the function can remediate any resource type across all projects.
column6: Create a dedicated service account with roles/storage.admin on specific buckets and roles/compute.securityAdmin on specific projects, then assign this service account to the Cloud Run function.
column8: Following the principle of least privilege, you should create a dedicated service account with only the specific permissions needed for remediation tasks. By scoping permissions to specific resources (buckets, projects) rather than organization-wide, you limit the potential blast radius if the service account is compromised. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/concepts/iam

column2: Your organization wants to test the impact of implementing stricter VPC Service Controls perimeters to protect sensitive projects before enforcing them as part of your security hardening initiative. You need to understand what traffic would be blocked without disrupting current operations. What should you do?
column3: Create a duplicate test environment with identical configurations and implement the enforced perimeter there first.
column4: Enable VPC Flow Logs on all subnets and analyze the traffic patterns to determine what communications would be blocked by the perimeter.
column5: Configure the VPC Service Controls perimeter in dry run mode and analyze violation logs in Cloud Logging to identify requests that would be denied.
column6: Implement the enforced perimeter during a maintenance window and monitor for errors, then roll back if issues occur.
column8: Dry run mode logs violations as though the perimeters are enforced but does not prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to understand the impact on existing workloads and identify necessary access level configurations before enforcement. Violation logs can be queried in Cloud Logging for analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: You are hunting for evidence of data exfiltration attempts in your Google Cloud environment. You have enabled Data Access audit logs for BigQuery and stored them in a Cloud Logging bucket. You want to identify queries that accessed tables containing sensitive data and wrote results to external projects. What is the most effective method to analyze these logs?
column3: Configure Event Threat Detection to automatically detect BigQuery data exfiltration by enabling the exfiltration detector module.
column4: Export the audit logs to Cloud Storage and use Cloud Data Loss Prevention to scan the logs for sensitive data patterns.
column5: Use the Logs Explorer with a filter for bigquery.googleapis.com/data_access and manually review each log entry for suspicious activity.
column6: Use Log Analytics SQL queries to filter Data Access logs for BigQuery jobs where the destination table project differs from the source table project.
column8: Log Analytics allows you to write SQL queries to analyze the structured fields in BigQuery audit logs. You can filter for InsertJob events and compare the source and destination project fields to identify cross-project data movements. The protoPayload.metadata fields contain detailed job configuration information for this analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-and-view

column2: Your organization has enabled Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) curated detections in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You receive an alert indicating an IOC match with 'Active Breach' priority. According to the ATI priority model, what does this priority level indicate about the matched indicator?
column3: The indicator has a Malicious GTI Verdict and High GTI Severity but has low prevalence in the threat landscape.
column4: The indicator is associated with threat actors or malware identified by Google Threat Intelligence but was not observed in active investigations.
column5: The indicator was blocked by security controls in other environments, suggesting it is a known commodity threat with broad targeting.
column6: The indicator was observed by Mandiant in active or past compromises with a Malicious GTI Verdict and High GTI Severity.
column8: The Active Breach model in ATI prioritizes indicators that Mandiant observed in active or past compromise investigations. The model uses features including GTI Verdict (Malicious), GTI Severity (High), Active IR status, Prevalence, and Attribution to assign this highest priority level. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: During an active security incident, your forensics team has collected evidence including disk images and exported logs into a Cloud Storage bucket. The legal department has informed you that a litigation hold is now in effect, requiring all collected evidence to be preserved indefinitely until further notice. The bucket already has a 90-day retention policy that is not locked. What should you do to comply with the litigation hold?
column3: Increase the bucket's retention policy to 100 years and then lock the retention policy.
column4: Lock the bucket's existing 90-day retention policy to make it permanent.
column5: Apply a temporary hold to each object in the bucket that is subject to the litigation.
column6: Create a new bucket with Object Retention Lock enabled and copy all evidence objects with locked retention configurations.
column8: Temporary holds prevent objects from being deleted regardless of their retention status or retention policy. Temporary holds remain in place until explicitly removed, making them ideal for litigation holds where the duration is unknown. When the litigation ends, the holds can be released without affecting the underlying retention policy. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/object-holds

column2: Your organization has received threat intelligence about a new malware campaign using specific IP addresses for command and control (C2) communication. You need to immediately check whether any assets in your environment have communicated with these IP addresses over the past 30 days using Google Security Operations (SecOps). What should you do?
column3: Use UDM Search with a query specifying the suspicious IP addresses in the target.ip or principal.ip fields, and set the time range to 30 days.
column4: Export logs to BigQuery and run SQL queries to search for the IP addresses across all tables over the 30-day period.
column5: Configure Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) to add these IP addresses and wait for automatic IoC matching to identify historical communications.
column6: Run a retrohunt using a YARA-L rule that monitors for real-time connections to the suspicious IP addresses from newly ingested logs.
column8: UDM Search allows you to find events in your Google SecOps instance using YARA-L 2.0 syntax against indexed fields like IP addresses. This is the most direct method to search for communication with known malicious IPs across your historical data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/investigation/udm-search

column2: Your organization wants to establish an identity baseline in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to detect anomalous user login behavior. You need to ingest Cloud Identity audit logs that capture user sign-in events including failed logins and suspicious login attempts. Which Cloud Identity audit log type should you prioritize for ingestion?
column3: Login Audit logs
column4: OAuth Token Audit logs
column5: Admin Audit logs
column6: SAML Audit logs
column8: Login Audit logs track user sign-ins to your domain and capture login events including Failed Login and Suspicious Login events. These events directly support establishing user authentication baselines for detecting anomalous login behavior. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/logs-based-security-alerting-in-google-cloud

column2: A project administrator reports that after an organization policy change was made 5 minutes ago, they can still create resources that should be restricted by the new policy. You need to determine why the policy is not yet effective. What is the most likely explanation?
column3: The project administrator has the Organization Policy Administrator role, which exempts them from policy enforcement.
column4: The project has a local organization policy that overrides the parent policy with inheritance disabled.
column5: Organization policy changes can take up to 15 minutes to be fully enforced across all resources.
column6: The organization policy was configured in dry-run mode instead of live enforcement mode.
column8: Changes to organization policies have an eventual consistency model and can take up to 15 minutes to propagate and be fully enforced. During this window, some operations that violate the new policy may still succeed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/using-constraints

column2: Your security team needs to detect exploitation attempts targeting web vulnerabilities in your organization's App Engine, GKE, and Compute Engine web applications. You want to enable automated scanning that detects OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities including cross-site scripting and SQL injection attacks. The solution must integrate with Security Command Center for centralized visibility. What should you do?
column3: Enable Web Security Scanner managed scans in Security Command Center to automatically run weekly scans on public web endpoints and surface findings in the Vulnerabilities page.
column4: Deploy Cloud Armor with preconfigured WAF rules to automatically generate Security Command Center findings when OWASP vulnerabilities are detected.
column5: Enable Container Threat Detection to scan web application containers for cross-site scripting and SQL injection vulnerabilities during runtime.
column6: Configure Event Threat Detection to monitor Cloud Logging streams and detect web application exploitation attempts based on HTTP request patterns.
column8: Web Security Scanner is a built-in Security Command Center service that identifies common vulnerabilities in App Engine, GKE, and Compute Engine web applications. Managed scans automatically run once each week to detect and scan public web endpoints and findings are automatically available in Security Command Center. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-web-security-scanner-overview

column2: Your organization has Security Command Center Premium activated at the organization level. You create an Event Threat Detection custom module at the organization level to detect connections to threat actor infrastructure. A project team asks why the custom module is generating findings in their project even though they did not create it. What explains this behavior?
column3: Custom modules only generate findings at the organization level, so findings must have been manually assigned to the project.
column4: Event Threat Detection custom modules must be explicitly enabled at each project level after creation at the organization level.
column5: Custom modules created at the organization level are inherited by all descendant folders and projects and automatically scan logs at those levels.
column6: The custom module was automatically replicated to the project when the project team enabled Event Threat Detection service.
column8: Custom modules created at a parent level (organization or folder) are inherited by child resources. When you're in the organization view, residential modules are those created at the organization level, and these become inherited modules at any folder or project level. This inheritance model ensures consistent threat detection across the entire organization hierarchy. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: You need to create a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to visualize security infrastructure metrics for your organization. The dashboard should display the current error budget remaining for your security API service, allow analysts to quickly identify whether the service is meeting its SLO, and show error budget consumption trends. Which combination of dashboard widgets provides the most effective visualization?
column3: Add a top list table showing all services ranked by error count, with conditional formatting to highlight services with high error rates.
column4: Create multiple stacked bar charts showing daily error counts, weekly compliance ratios, and monthly error budget allocation across all services.
column5: Configure a single heatmap widget that displays all SLO metrics including error budget, compliance status, and consumption trends in a single view.
column6: Add a scorecard widget showing current error budget percentage, a gauge widget displaying SLO compliance status, and a line chart showing error budget consumption over time.
column8: Scorecards display a single numeric value (error budget percentage) for quick reference, gauge widgets provide visual indication of current performance against thresholds, and line charts show trends over time. This combination addresses all three requirements effectively. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/dashboards/api-examples

column2: Your organization's threat intelligence team has received a new set of malicious IP addresses associated with a recent APT campaign. You want to determine if any historical connections to these IP addresses occurred in your environment over the past 90 days using Google Security Operations (SecOps). What should you do?
column3: Use the Alerts and IoCs page to filter for the malicious IP addresses and review the automatically matched IOC history.
column4: Configure Applied Threat Intelligence to automatically analyze the 90-day historical data for the new IP addresses.
column5: Export all network logs to BigQuery and run a SQL query to search for the malicious IP addresses.
column6: Create a YARA-L detection rule that matches the malicious IP addresses against network events, and run a retrohunt over the 90-day time range.
column8: Retrohunt lets you use a selected rule to search for detections throughout existing data in Google SecOps. By creating a YARA-L rule matching the malicious IP addresses and running it against historical data, you can identify any past connections to those indicators within the specified time range. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: You are configuring alerting for a user-defined log-based counter metric that monitors security-related errors. During testing, you notice the alerting policy generates false-positive notifications due to gaps in metric data when no errors occur. What should you do to reduce false notifications while maintaining detection accuracy?
column3: Increase the rolling window duration for the alerting policy condition to at least 10 minutes to allow for data point aggregation across gaps.
column4: Convert the counter metric to a distribution metric to better handle sparse data scenarios.
column5: Create multiple alerting policies with different thresholds to cross-validate the alerts before sending notifications.
column6: Configure the alerting policy to use 'missing data is bad' in the advanced options to treat gaps as zero values.
column8: Log-based metric data can have gaps when no matching log entries occur, and these gaps can cause false notifications. Google Cloud recommends selecting a rolling window value of at least 10 minutes, especially to ensure multiple log entries that match your filter are counted and to reduce the risk of false notifications from data gaps. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/charts-and-alerts

column2: You are building a post-incident trend analysis report to identify patterns across security incidents over the past 12 months. Your organization uses Google SecOps Enterprise Plus and wants to correlate rule detections with IOC matches to understand attack trends. Which BigQuery tables should you query to build this analysis?
column3: Query the entity_graph table to retrieve all entities involved in incidents and manually correlate them with external threat intelligence feeds.
column4: Query the udm_events table exclusively and use YARA-L pattern matching within BigQuery to identify detection trends.
column5: Query the ingestion_metrics table and calculate detection rates by comparing ingested log volumes against alert counts.
column6: Query the rule_detections table for detection patterns and the ioc_matches table for indicator correlations from the Google SecOps BigQuery datalake dataset.
column8: Google SecOps exports rule_detections (which stores detections returned by rules) and ioc_matches (which stores IOC matches found against UDM events) to BigQuery. Correlating these tables provides comprehensive attack trend analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: You need to perform retroactive threat hunting across historical VPC Flow Logs data to search for indicators of compromise (IOCs) involving specific malicious IP addresses. Your VPC Flow Logs are stored in Cloud Logging with a 30-day retention period. You need to query logs older than 30 days. What is the recommended approach?
column3: Export the VPC Flow Logs to a Cloud Storage bucket using a log sink before the retention period expires, then query the exported JSON files directly using BigQuery external tables.
column4: Query the VPC Flow Logs directly using Logs Explorer with filters for the specific IP addresses, as Logs Explorer automatically archives data beyond the retention period for security investigations.
column5: Use Google SecOps SIEM retrohunt capabilities to search for the IOCs across historical VPC Flow Logs, as SecOps maintains separate long-term retention independent of Cloud Logging settings.
column6: Before the 30-day retention expires, upgrade the log bucket to use Log Analytics, create a linked BigQuery dataset, and extend the bucket retention period to store logs for the required historical period.
column8: Upgrading to Log Analytics with a linked BigQuery dataset enables SQL-based querying while logs remain stored in Cloud Logging. Extending the retention period beyond the default 30 days ensures historical data is available for retroactive threat hunting. This approach provides cost-effective storage with analytical capabilities. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Your security team detected that a developer has been granted the Service Account Token Creator role at the project level, which allows them to impersonate any service account in the project. You need to restrict this access following the principle of least privilege while still allowing the developer to impersonate a specific service account for local development. What should you do?
column3: Remove the project-level Service Account Token Creator role binding and grant the role on only the specific service account the developer needs to impersonate.
column4: Create a custom role that includes only the iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken permission and grant it at the organization level.
column5: Keep the project-level Service Account Token Creator role but add an IAM Condition that restricts impersonation to business hours only.
column6: Remove all impersonation permissions from the developer and create a service account key for them to use for local development instead.
column8: Granting the Service Account Token Creator role at the service account level rather than the project level follows least privilege. This restricts impersonation capability to only the specific service account needed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-permissions

column2: Your organization is configuring a Cloud Logging sink to route security logs to BigQuery for threat intelligence enrichment at scale. Security analysts will run daily queries that JOIN log data with a threat intelligence IOC table containing IP addresses and domain indicators. You need to optimize the log data table for query performance and cost efficiency when correlating logs with IOCs. What should you do?
column3: Create the log sink with date-sharded tables as the default configuration, then use wildcard table functions to query across multiple daily shards.
column4: Create the log sink targeting a Cloud Storage bucket first, then configure external tables in BigQuery to query the logs without ingestion costs.
column5: Create the log sink with partitioned tables enabled and partition by ingestion time, then use the _PARTITIONTIME pseudo-column in queries to limit data scans.
column6: Create the log sink with a linked dataset from a Log Analytics-enabled log bucket to avoid BigQuery streaming and storage costs.
column8: Partitioning is recommended over table sharding as partitioned tables perform better. Queries that specify predicate filters on the _PARTITIONTIME pseudo-column limit the amount of logs scanned, reducing costs and improving performance for threat intelligence correlation queries. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: Your SOC team manages multiple client environments using Google SecOps SOAR and frequently reuses the same communication workflow for notifying clients about security incidents. The workflow includes sending an email, waiting for client acknowledgment, and then updating the case stage. You want to implement this workflow efficiently across multiple playbooks while ensuring that changes to the workflow are automatically reflected everywhere it is used. What should you do?
column3: Create a playbook block with input parameters for communication type and method, then insert this block into each parent playbook where the workflow is needed.
column4: Export the communication workflow as a JSON template and import it into each new playbook using the Content Hub integration package feature.
column5: Duplicate the communication playbook for each client environment and maintain separate versions with environment-specific configurations.
column6: Configure a use case from the Content Hub that includes the communication workflow and deploy it to each environment with custom parameters.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that can be incorporated into multiple parent playbooks. Any changes made to a block automatically affect all playbooks that use it, ensuring consistent workflow updates across all implementations. Input parameters allow customization per instance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Detection engineering"You are configuring curated detections in Google Security Operations (SecOps) and notice that a Windows threat detection rule set is generating excessive alerts for activity in your development environment. You want to reduce false positives while maintaining detection coverage for production systems. What should you do?
column3: Disable the entire curated detection rule set and create custom YARA-L rules that include filters for production systems only.
column4: Modify the alerting threshold in the curated detection settings to increase the severity level required before generating alerts.
column5: Configure rule exclusions for the curated detection rule set to exclude events from development environment hostnames or asset groups.
column6: Set the curated detection to 'detect only' mode and create a composite detection rule that filters out development environment alerts.
column8: Curated detections support rule exclusions that allow you to specify criteria to prevent certain events from being evaluated by a rule or rule set. This enables you to reduce detection volume from specific environments while maintaining full coverage elsewhere. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/curated-detections

column2: Your security team wants to configure Security Command Center to export Event Threat Detection and Container Threat Detection findings to Cloud Logging for centralized analysis. Your organization has Security Command Center Premium activated at the project level. When you navigate to SCC Settings, you do not see the option to configure logging export. What should you do to enable this capability?
column3: Contact Google Cloud support to enable the logging export feature flag for project-level Premium activations.
column4: Upgrade to an organization-level activation of Security Command Center Premium, as Cloud Logging export requires organization-level activation.
column5: Enable the Cloud Logging API in the project and grant the Security Command Center service account the Logs Writer role.
column6: Create a custom Pub/Sub topic and configure a Cloud Logging sink to route SCC findings to the topic.
column8: Continuous exports to Cloud Logging are only available when you activate Security Command Center at the organization level. Project-level activations do not support this feature regardless of the tier. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/export-cloud-logging

column2: Your organization is implementing security monitoring in Google Security Operations and needs to ingest Cloud Identity audit logs to establish identity behavior baselines. You want to track group membership changes that could indicate privilege escalation attempts. Which configuration approach provides the required visibility?
column3: Configure the Cloud Identity API feed in Google SecOps SOAR and enable real-time group membership change monitoring.
column4: Deploy a Google SecOps forwarder on your domain controller to capture Cloud Identity group membership events directly.
column5: Enable Google Workspace data sharing with Google Cloud, then configure a sink to export Groups audit logs and Admin audit logs to Google SecOps.
column6: Enable Data Access audit logs for Cloud Identity and configure automatic export to Google SecOps using the GCP_CLOUDAUDIT parser.
column8: To view and export Cloud Identity audit logs in Google Cloud, you must first enable sharing of Google Workspace data with Google Cloud. After enabling this sharing, Google Cloud receives all audit logs for Google Workspace including Groups audit logs that track changes to group memberships and Admin audit logs that track group-related events performed in the Admin Console. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit/configure-gsuite-audit-logs

column2: You are deploying Security Command Center Enterprise and need to configure the SCC Enterprise - Cloud Orchestration and Remediation use case for your organization. The organization uses ServiceNow for IT service management. You need to enable automatic ticket creation for posture findings while ensuring the correct playbook is active. What should you do?
column3: Enable both the Posture Findings - Generic playbook and the Posture Findings with SNOW playbook to ensure findings are processed even if ServiceNow integration fails.
column4: Disable the Posture Findings - Generic playbook, enable the Posture Findings with SNOW playbook, and configure the ServiceNow integration with the custom ticket type.
column5: Configure the SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector to send findings directly to ServiceNow using webhook integration without modifying playbook settings.
column6: Create a custom playbook that uses the ServiceNow API to create tickets, then attach it to all posture finding alerts using tag-based triggers.
column8: When integrating with ticketing systems like ServiceNow, you must disable the generic playbook and enable the ticketing-system-specific playbook. The Posture Findings with SNOW playbook is designed to work with ServiceNow integration and handles ticket creation and synchronization. You also need to create the custom SCC Enterprise Cloud Posture Ticket type in ServiceNow. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/integrate-ticketing-systems

column2: You have deployed a Cloud Function triggered by Pub/Sub to process threat intelligence feeds and automatically search for IOCs in your Google SecOps environment. During testing, you notice that some threat intelligence messages are being dropped when the function experiences transient errors. You need to ensure that all threat intelligence updates are processed without losing any messages. What should you do?
column3: Deploy multiple instances of the Cloud Function in different regions and configure Pub/Sub to publish messages to all instances simultaneously for redundancy.
column4: Enable exactly-once delivery on the Pub/Sub subscription to guarantee that each threat intelligence message is processed exactly one time without any losses.
column5: Configure a dead-letter topic for the Pub/Sub subscription associated with the Eventarc trigger, and set appropriate retry policies with exponential backoff.
column6: Increase the function memory allocation and timeout settings to ensure the function has sufficient resources to process all threat intelligence messages without errors.
column8: Configuring a dead-letter topic ensures that messages that cannot be successfully delivered within the message retention window are forwarded for later analysis rather than being discarded. Combined with retry policies, this provides resilient message processing. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/eventarc/docs/retry-events

column2: You are deploying a new organization policy to restrict VM creation to only Confidential VMs across your organization. Before enforcing this policy in production, you want to understand which existing resources would be affected without blocking any operations. What should you do?
column3: Set the organization policy with 'enforce: true' and immediately set 'enforce: false' to capture logs of initial violations.
column4: Configure the organization policy in dry-run mode using dryRunSpec to audit violations without blocking operations.
column5: Use Policy Simulator to test the organization policy impact on all existing VMs in the organization.
column6: Deploy the policy to a test folder first and manually verify which VMs would be non-compliant by checking configurations.
column8: Organization policies can be deployed in dry-run mode, which logs violations to Cloud Audit Logs without actually denying the violating actions. This allows you to assess the impact of the policy change in your production environment before full enforcement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/dry-run-policy

column2: You are configuring Security Command Center to improve vulnerability prioritization. You want attack exposure scores to accurately reflect your organization's security priorities for resources containing sensitive customer data. Currently, SCC is generating attack exposure scores but they do not align with your business risk profile. What should you do?
column3: Create resource value configurations that assign HIGH priority values to resources that match attributes for your sensitive data systems.
column4: Enable Sensitive Data Protection discovery to automatically identify and tag all resources with sensitive data as high priority for attack exposure scoring.
column5: Modify the severity levels of vulnerability findings in Security Command Center to match your organization's risk tolerance.
column6: Configure Event Threat Detection to increase detection priority for resources containing sensitive customer data.
column8: Resource value configurations let you designate specific resources as high-value based on attributes like resource type, project, or tags. When you assign priority values (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH), Risk Engine calculates attack exposure scores that reflect how vulnerabilities expose these designated high-value resources to potential attacks. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-learn

column2: Your organization wants to establish a sensitive data classification baseline using Cloud DLP that includes detection of organization-specific identifiers not covered by built-in infoTypes. These identifiers follow a consistent pattern of three letters followed by six digits (e.g., ABC123456). Which approach should you use to implement this detection?
column3: Submit a feature request to Google to add your organization's identifier format as a new built-in infoType detector.
column4: Use the DLP API's hotword rules to boost likelihood scores when the three-letter prefix appears near numeric sequences in your data.
column5: Create a custom infoType detector using a regular expression pattern in the inspection template and include it in your discovery scan configuration.
column6: Configure a stored custom dictionary detector with all possible combinations of the identifier pattern stored in a Cloud Storage bucket.
column8: Sensitive Data Protection allows you to create custom infoType detectors using regular expressions that can be included in inspection templates. By defining a regex pattern like '[A-Z]{3}[0-9]{6}' and adding it to your inspection configuration, the discovery service will detect these organization-specific identifiers alongside built-in infoTypes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/creating-custom-infotypes

column2: You are reviewing service account permissions in your organization and notice that multiple service accounts have been granted the Editor role at the project level. Several of these service accounts have not used most of the permissions in the past 90 days. You want to implement least privilege without disrupting existing workloads. What should you do?
column3: Immediately revoke the Editor role from all service accounts and grant only the Viewer role until workloads explicitly request additional permissions.
column4: Configure organization policy constraints to disable service account creation and use the default Compute Engine service account for all workloads.
column5: Create a custom role with all permissions from the Editor role except those flagged as sensitive, then replace the Editor role with this custom role.
column6: Review IAM Recommender role recommendations for each service account and apply the suggested predefined or custom roles that include only the permissions used by each service account.
column8: IAM Recommender analyzes permission usage and suggests smaller roles that cover only the permissions needed, helping achieve least privilege without causing disruptions. It uses ML to also predict permissions likely needed in the future. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/role-recommendations-overview

column2: Your threat hunting team is using Google Security Operations (SecOps) to investigate potential malicious activity. They have identified a new list of suspicious IP addresses from external threat intelligence sources. The team wants to search for any historical connections to these IP addresses across the past 90 days of ingested logs and receive results as quickly as possible. What should you do?
column3: Create a YARA-L rule with the suspicious IP addresses in a reference list and run a retrohunt for the past 90 days.
column4: Use UDM search with manual queries for each IP address individually across the time range.
column5: Create a YARA-L rule with the suspicious IP addresses in a reference list and enable the rule for live detection.
column6: Configure Applied Threat Intelligence to automatically ingest and match the IP addresses.
column8: Retrohunt enables running detection rules against historical data within your retention period. Using a reference list with the suspicious IP addresses allows efficient matching, and retrohunts can scan all historical UDM events to identify any past connections to those IOCs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: You need to create a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM dashboard that visualizes detection counts grouped by severity over time. You want to configure the chart to display results for the past 30 days. Which YARA-L query structure is correct for this dashboard visualization?
column3: Create a multi-event rule with a 30-day time window in the match section and severity-based conditions to generate detection statistics.
column4: Use timestamp.get_date on detection.created_time.seconds and match on $date and $severity with count_distinct aggregation in the outcome section.
column5: Query the detection data source using the detection prefix with events and condition sections to filter by severity over 30 days.
column6: Use a UDM search query with security_result.severity field filtering and export results to a chart widget.
column8: Dashboard YARA-L queries require extracting date from detection timestamps using timestamp.get_date, grouping by date and severity in the match section, and using aggregation functions like count_distinct in the outcome section. The query should reference detection fields directly without a condition section. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reference/sample-yaral-for-native-dashboard

column2: Your organization recently deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) and wants to identify brute force login attacks targeting user accounts. You need to configure the Risk Analytics dashboard to effectively detect short-term authentication anomalies while comparing current behavior against established baselines. What should you do?
column3: Set the Risk Calculation Window to 7 Days to allow more time for baselines to be established before detecting anomalous authentication patterns.
column4: Configure a custom 48-hour Risk Calculation Window to balance short-term and long-term detection requirements.
column5: Set the Risk Calculation Window to 24 Hours to detect patterns such as brute force attempts that occur over a short period compared to historical usage.
column6: Enable real-time entity risk scoring without any Risk Calculation Window to detect attacks as they occur.
column8: The 24-hour Risk Calculation Window is optimized for detecting short-term attacks like brute force login attempts. The Risk Analytics dashboard compares current entity behavior against historical baselines, and a shorter window better surfaces rapid authentication anomalies. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/risk-analytics-dashboard

column2: During incident response, you need to isolate a group of VMs that share a common service account. The VMs are running critical workloads and you want to implement containment using VPC firewall rules without requiring changes to each individual VM. Which approach provides the most efficient targeting mechanism for the firewall rule?
column3: Create a hierarchical firewall policy at the folder level with the deny rule targeting all instances in the folder.
column4: Assign a new network tag to each VM that needs to be isolated and create a firewall rule targeting that tag.
column5: Create a VPC firewall rule using target service accounts to apply the deny rule to all VMs running with the specified service account.
column6: Create a VPC firewall rule with source range set to the internal IP addresses of all VMs that need to be isolated.
column8: Service accounts provide an IAM-governed targeting mechanism that automatically applies to all VMs using that service account. Unlike network tags, service accounts cannot be modified by instance administrators without appropriate IAM permissions, making them more secure for incident response scenarios. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls

column2: Your organization wants to centralize all security-related audit logs from across 50 Google Cloud projects into a single Cloud Storage bucket for long-term retention and compliance auditing. You need to configure this with minimal ongoing maintenance as projects are added to the organization. What should you do?
column3: Create an aggregated sink at the organization level with an inclusion filter for audit logs and route to the Cloud Storage bucket.
column4: Configure the _Default sink in each project to route logs to the central Cloud Storage bucket.
column5: Create a sink in each of the 50 projects configured to route audit logs to the central Cloud Storage bucket.
column6: Create a Pub/Sub topic that collects logs from all projects and use a Cloud Function to write to Cloud Storage.
column8: Aggregated sinks at the organization level automatically collect logs from all child resources including folders and projects. Using the --include-children option ensures that log entries from all current and future projects within the organization are routed without requiring manual configuration for each new project. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks

column2: Your organization is deploying a new security-sensitive application on GKE and wants maximum workload isolation using GKE Sandbox. The security team also wants to enable Container Threat Detection to monitor for runtime threats. What should you advise the team regarding this configuration?
column3: Container Threat Detection is not compatible with GKE Sandbox and must be disabled on clusters where you want GKE Sandbox deployed for workload isolation.
column4: Deploy Container Threat Detection in passive monitoring mode which bypasses the kernel instrumentation requirement and relies solely on log analysis.
column5: Enable both features simultaneously and configure Container Threat Detection to use the GKE Sandbox API for collecting behavioral telemetry from sandboxed workloads.
column6: Configure Container Threat Detection at the node pool level and GKE Sandbox at the pod level to allow both features to coexist on the same cluster.
column8: Container Threat Detection requires access to kernel-level behavior in the guest kernel to detect threats. GKE Sandbox uses gVisor to provide an additional layer of defense by intercepting and handling system calls in userspace, which prevents Container Threat Detection from accessing the kernel data it needs. The features are mutually exclusive. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: Your organization has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) to perform threat hunting across your multi-cloud environment that includes Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure. You receive intelligence about a newly discovered threat actor that has been active for the past six months. You need to search for indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with this threat actor across your historical security telemetry. Which approach should you use?
column3: Use UDM Search to query the last 90 days of events and export results to BigQuery for extended historical analysis beyond the search limit.
column4: Create a YARA-L rule that matches the IOCs and run a retrohunt against 12 months of historical data to identify any past matches.
column5: Configure curated detections to automatically match the new IOCs in real-time and rely on future alerts to identify compromised assets.
column6: Export all raw logs to Cloud Storage and use BigQuery to perform pattern matching queries across the full retention period.
column8: Google SecOps retains 12 months of hot data by default and retrohunts enable searching historical data using detection rules. This approach allows comprehensive scanning of historical telemetry against newly discovered IOCs associated with the threat actor. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your threat hunting team wants to create a custom Event Threat Detection module to monitor for connections to malicious domains identified in recent threat intelligence reports. You need to configure the module using the gcloud CLI. What information must be included in the JSON template for the Configurable Bad Domain custom module?
column3: A YARA-L rule definition specifying domain matching conditions and a correlation window for detecting repeated connections.
column4: A CEL expression defining the domain matching logic and a resource_types array specifying which Google Cloud resources to monitor.
column5: A metadata section containing severity, description, and recommendation fields, along with a domains list specifying the malicious domains to monitor.
column6: A detection_rules section with regex patterns for domain matching and a threshold configuration for alert frequency tuning.
column8: The JSON template for Configurable Bad Domain custom modules requires a metadata section that defines severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), description, and recommendation for remediation. It also requires the domains parameter listing the web domains to watch for in Cloud DNS Logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: You are configuring security alerting for your Google Cloud environment. You need to be notified immediately when a human user accesses the security key of a service account, as this indicates potential credential compromise. Which Cloud Logging alerting approach should you use?
column3: Create a user-defined log-based counter metric that counts CreateServiceAccountKey events and configure a threshold-based alert when count exceeds zero.
column4: Create a log-based alerting policy with a filter matching the CreateServiceAccountKey method in Admin Activity audit logs.
column5: Use the Logs Explorer to create a saved query for service account key creation and manually review results each hour.
column6: Configure a SQL-based alerting policy in Log Analytics with a 5-minute lookback window that queries for service account key creation events.
column8: Log-based alerting policies are designed for catching security-related events in individual log entries, such as when a human user accesses a service account key. Log-based alerting policies use the LogMatch condition type and can include data from the log entry in notifications. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/alerting/log-based-alerts

column2: Your organization runs critical workloads on GKE clusters and wants to enable Container Threat Detection to monitor for file-based attacks such as modifications to PAM configuration files and sensitive file access. However, you are concerned about potential performance impacts on workloads with high file I/O. What should you consider when configuring Container Threat Detection?
column3: File monitoring detectors are enabled by default with Container Threat Detection. Disable them on clusters with high file I/O workloads to prevent performance degradation.
column4: Container Threat Detection file monitoring is only available through GKE Sandbox and requires enabling that feature first on clusters before file detectors can be activated.
column5: Container Threat Detection has no performance impact on workloads. Enable all detectors including file monitoring without any performance evaluation required.
column6: File monitoring detectors are disabled by default in Container Threat Detection. Enable them selectively and evaluate performance impact on workloads before deploying in production.
column8: Container Threat Detection file monitoring detectors that monitor access or modification to critical system files are disabled by default to avoid unexpected performance impacts on high file I/O workloads like CI/CD systems. Organizations should evaluate the impact before enabling these detectors. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your security team needs to view the historical state of cloud assets from 30 days ago to investigate a potential security incident. You want to retrieve a point-in-time snapshot of asset configurations. Which Cloud Asset Inventory feature should you use?
column3: Query the Cloud Audit Logs for all asset modifications in the past 30 days and reconstruct the asset state from the change events.
column4: Configure a Cloud Asset Inventory feed to replay historical Pub/Sub messages from the past 30 days using message retention settings.
column5: Enable versioning on the Cloud Asset Inventory export destination bucket and retrieve the asset file version from 30 days ago.
column6: Use the export or list assets API with the snapshot-time parameter set to the desired historical timestamp, which supports up to 35 days in the past.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory maintains asset history for up to 35 days. When using export or list operations, you can specify a snapshot-time parameter to retrieve asset state at a specific point in time within this window. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/asset-inventory-overview

column2: You are investigating a multi-stage attack using Google Security Operations (SecOps) and need to correlate authentication failures with subsequent suspicious process executions from the same host within a 10-minute window. Which approach best supports this investigation requirement?
column3: Use the sliding window feature with the 'after' keyword to check for process executions that occur before authentication failures.
column4: Write a multi-event YARA-L rule using the match section with a 10-minute time window and correlate events using the principal.hostname field.
column5: Configure an outcome variable to set severity based on the count of authentication failures without time-based correlation.
column6: Create separate single-event rules for authentication failures and process executions, then manually correlate results in a dashboard.
column8: Multi-event YARA-L rules allow correlation across different event types using match variables and time windows. By joining on principal.hostname and specifying a 10-minute window in the match section, you can detect the sequence of authentication failures followed by suspicious process executions on the same host. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-overview

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise with integrated case management. A case containing multiple Security Health Analytics vulnerability findings has a mix of HIGH and MEDIUM severity findings. The security team needs to understand how the case priority is determined. What describes how Security Command Center sets case priority?
column3: Case priority is set manually by the security analyst during initial triage and remains static throughout the case lifecycle.
column4: Case priority is determined by the first finding ingested into the case and does not change regardless of subsequent findings added.
column5: Case priority is calculated as an average of all finding severities within the case, rounded to the nearest severity level.
column6: Case priority is automatically set based on the highest finding severity among all findings in the case, and updates dynamically if the severity changes.
column8: Case priority is based on the highest finding severity in the case. When the finding severity changes, Security Command Center automatically updates the case priority to match the highest severity property among all findings in a case. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/cases-overview

column2: You are managing Security Health Analytics for a large enterprise with Security Command Center activated at the organization level. Your team reports that vulnerability findings for newly created Google Cloud resources appear with a delay of up to 24 hours. You need to reduce the detection latency for configuration changes. What should you understand about Security Health Analytics scan behavior?
column3: Security Health Analytics supports real-time scans for Google Cloud resources that start whenever a change is detected in a resource's configuration, writing findings immediately to Security Command Center.
column4: Security Health Analytics performs real-time scans for all resource types on both Google Cloud and AWS environments, with findings appearing within minutes of configuration changes.
column5: Security Health Analytics only supports batch mode scanning that runs once every 24 hours, and real-time detection requires enabling Event Threat Detection instead.
column6: Security Health Analytics real-time scanning requires enabling VPC Flow Logs and Data Access audit logs, which then trigger immediate vulnerability assessments when resources are modified.
column8: Security Health Analytics operates in multiple scan modes for Google Cloud deployments. Real-time scans are triggered by resource configuration changes and write findings to Security Command Center immediately. However, not all detectors support real-time scanning, and batch scans run once daily as a complement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-security-health-analytics

column2: Detection engineering"You are configuring an Event Threat Detection custom module for Configurable Bad IP detection and need to specify the parameters for the module. Which metadata elements must be included in the JSON template to properly configure the custom module?
column3: The template requires only the ips array with IP addresses, as severity and description are automatically assigned based on Google's threat intelligence scoring.
column4: The metadata section must include severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), description, and recommendation fields, along with the ips array containing the IP addresses or CIDR ranges to detect.
column5: The template must include the MITRE ATT&CK tactic and technique mappings, finding category name, and the ips array for proper correlation with threat frameworks.
column6: The template requires enablement_state, project_id, and organization_id fields in the metadata section to define the scope of the custom module detection.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom module templates require a metadata section with severity, description, and recommendation fields that define how findings are categorized and what remediation guidance is provided. For the Configurable Bad IP module type specifically, you must also include an ips array containing the IP addresses or CIDR ranges that should trigger findings when detected in VPC Flow Logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: You have deployed a Cloud Function that processes threat intelligence updates from a Pub/Sub subscription and calls the Google SecOps Ingestion API to add new IOCs to reference lists. During testing, you observe that some IOC updates are being processed multiple times, causing duplicate entries in reference lists. You need to modify your implementation to prevent duplicate processing while maintaining reliable message delivery. What should you do?
column3: Configure the Pub/Sub subscription with a longer acknowledgment deadline and disable message retention so that unacknowledged messages are automatically deleted after the deadline expires.
column4: Implement idempotent processing logic in the Cloud Function by checking if the IOC already exists in the reference list before adding it, and ensure the function returns successfully only after the IOC is confirmed to be stored.
column5: Reduce the Cloud Function timeout to 10 seconds to ensure fast message acknowledgment and prevent the Pub/Sub service from redelivering messages that take too long to process.
column6: Configure the Pub/Sub subscription to use exactly-once delivery mode, which guarantees that each message is delivered and processed exactly one time without requiring any application changes.
column8: Pub/Sub guarantees at-least-once delivery, so functions must be idempotent to handle potential redeliveries. Checking for existing IOCs before adding and confirming successful storage ensures duplicates are prevented while maintaining reliability. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/writing/write-event-driven-functions

column2: Your threat intelligence team has identified new IOCs associated with an advanced persistent threat (APT) campaign. You need to determine if these IOCs were present in your environment over the past 30 days using Google Security Operations (SecOps). You have created a YARA-L detection rule that matches these IOCs. What should you do?
column3: Enable the detection rule as a live rule and wait for it to process the historical data backlog automatically within 24 hours.
column4: Use UDM Search with the IOC values as search terms and manually review the results for the past 30 days.
column5: Run a retrohunt using the new detection rule against the past 30 days of historical data to search for matches in previously ingested events.
column6: Export all UDM events from the past 30 days to BigQuery and run SQL queries matching the IOCs against the exported data.
column8: Retrohunt is designed to run detection rules against historical data in Google SecOps. It allows you to search for IOCs across previously ingested events to determine if the threat was present before the rule was created. Retrohunts can search data within the retention period. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization has a large-scale Google Cloud environment with thousands of projects and needs to perform complex asset analysis across all projects. Security analysts are experiencing timeouts when using the Cloud Asset Inventory list API. What is the recommended approach to handle this at scale?
column3: Use the SearchAllResources API from the Google Cloud console to search assets more efficiently than the list API.
column4: Export asset metadata to BigQuery using the Cloud Asset Inventory export API, then run SQL queries against the exported data.
column5: Split the organization into smaller scopes and run parallel list API requests across each folder individually.
column6: Increase the page size parameter in list requests to the maximum of 500 to reduce the number of API calls needed.
column8: For large-scale environments, the Cloud Asset Inventory list API may not meet performance requirements and can result in timeouts. The recommended approach is to export data to BigQuery, which is designed for large-scale data analysis and supports complex SQL queries. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/list-assets

column2: Detection engineering"Your organization has enabled Web Security Scanner in Security Command Center and is receiving findings. A recent scan identified an XSS vulnerability categorized as 'XSS_ERROR' in a critical web application. The development team has requested details to reproduce and remediate the finding. What information should you provide to help them remediate this vulnerability?
column3: Generate a compliance report showing the XSS finding mapped to OWASP standards and provide remediation guidance based on the compliance framework.
column4: Provide the scan logs from Cloud Logging that show all requests made during the scan to identify which input vectors were tested.
column5: Share the finding's Reproduction URL from Security Command Center which contains the exact request including payload parameters that triggered the XSS detection.
column6: Export the finding JSON and send the full vulnerability definition including all metadata fields and associated asset information.
column8: Web Security Scanner findings include a Reproduction URL that allows developers to recreate the exact conditions that triggered the vulnerability detection. For XSS findings, this URL contains the test payload that the scanner used when detecting the vulnerability, enabling developers to verify and remediate the issue. This is the most actionable information for remediation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-remediate-web-security-scanner-findings

column2: Your organization is configuring Google SecOps SOAR to automate endpoint isolation through an EDR integration. The security team requires that endpoint isolation actions be reviewed and approved by a senior analyst before execution, while all enrichment actions should run automatically. How should you configure the playbook actions?
column3: Create separate playbooks for isolation and enrichment, with the isolation playbook requiring manual trigger.
column4: Configure a flow condition before the isolation action that waits for external approval via email.
column5: Use the Time to respond setting on all actions to ensure analysts have time to review before execution.
column6: Set the endpoint isolation action type to Manual with a SOC role assignment, and keep enrichment actions set to Automatic.
column8: Setting an action to Manual requires human approval before execution. Assigning the action to a SOC role ensures it appears in the Pending Actions widget for senior analysts to review. Enrichment actions can remain automatic since they only gather data without making changes to endpoints. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-actions-in-playbooks

column2: Your organization is building an automated threat hunting system using Cloud Functions triggered by threat intelligence updates from a Pub/Sub topic. The function calls the Google SecOps API to perform retrohunts based on new IOCs. During testing, you observe that the function occasionally times out when the SecOps API is slow to respond. You need to ensure reliable processing without losing threat intelligence updates. What should you do?
column3: Set the Pub/Sub subscription acknowledgment deadline to its maximum value of 600 seconds.
column4: Configure the Cloud Function to store the IOC payload in Cloud Storage and return success immediately, then process asynchronously.
column5: Enable automatic retries with exponential backoff and configure a dead-letter topic to capture messages that exceed maximum delivery attempts.
column6: Increase the Cloud Function timeout to 9 minutes to ensure the SecOps API call always completes.
column8: Combining automatic retries with exponential backoff handles transient failures like API slowdowns, while the dead-letter topic captures messages that fail repeatedly after multiple attempts. This ensures no threat intelligence updates are lost and provides a mechanism for manual review of failed messages. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/functions/docs/bestpractices/retries

column2: Your organization must generate weekly compliance reports showing all IAM policy changes across the entire Google Cloud organization. The reports need to be stored in BigQuery for historical analysis and must run automatically without manual intervention. You have already configured an aggregated sink to route audit logs to a BigQuery dataset. What should you do next to meet these requirements?
column3: Configure Cloud Logging to create log-based metrics for IAM changes and export the metrics to BigQuery using Cloud Monitoring.
column4: Use Logs Explorer to manually export IAM change events weekly and configure email notifications for the exported results.
column5: Create a BigQuery scheduled query that filters protoPayload.methodName for SetIamPolicy events and writes results to a destination table with WRITE_APPEND.
column6: Create a Cloud Scheduler job that triggers a Cloud Function to query the logs and store results in Cloud Storage as CSV files.
column8: BigQuery scheduled queries allow you to automate recurring SQL queries that can run on a defined schedule. Using WRITE_APPEND ensures historical data is preserved for compliance purposes. Filtering on protoPayload.methodName allows you to specifically target IAM policy change events in the audit logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/scheduling-queries

column2: Your security team is developing a YARA-L detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to identify suspicious DNS queries to IP addresses from a known threat intelligence list. The rule is experiencing performance issues due to the large volume of events being evaluated. You need to optimize the rule without changing the detection logic. What should you do?
column3: Move the reference list check to the condition section instead of the events section.
column4: Increase the match window size to reduce the frequency of rule execution.
column5: Create a separate reference list for each threat category and split the rule into multiple smaller rules.
column6: Add an event type filter for NETWORK_DNS at the beginning of the events section before referencing the reference list.
column8: Adding an event type filter can optimize your rule by reducing the number of events the rule needs to evaluate. Placing this filter at the beginning of the events section ensures that filtering happens first. This is a recommended YARA-L best practice. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-best-practices

column2: Your organization uses Shared VPC with a host project and multiple service projects. You are configuring a VPC Service Controls perimeter to protect Cloud Storage buckets in the service projects. After creating the perimeter with only the service projects, users inside the VPC network cannot access the protected Cloud Storage resources. What should you do to resolve this issue?
column3: Enable VPC accessible services and set it to 'All services' for the perimeter containing the service projects.
column4: Create a perimeter bridge between the host project perimeter and the service projects perimeter to allow communication.
column5: Add the Shared VPC host project to the same service perimeter as the service projects.
column6: Configure an ingress rule to allow traffic from the Shared VPC network to access the protected services in the service projects.
column8: When using Shared VPC, you must include the host project in a service perimeter along with any projects that belong to the Shared VPC. The VPC network belongs to the host project, so requests originating from VMs in the Shared VPC are considered as coming from the host project. If the host project is not in the perimeter, these requests are blocked. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/service-perimeters

column2: Your organization recently created new Google Cloud projects and you notice that the default Compute Engine service accounts are being granted the Editor role automatically. This violates your organization's least privilege security policy. You need to prevent this behavior for all future projects. What should you do?
column3: Enable the constraints/iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts organization policy constraint at the organization level.
column4: Disable the creation of default service accounts by enforcing the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountCreation organization policy constraint.
column5: Remove the Editor role from all existing default service accounts and document the requirement for project administrators to follow least privilege.
column6: Configure a Cloud Function triggered by project creation events to automatically revoke the Editor role from default service accounts.
column8: This organization policy constraint prevents default service accounts from automatically being granted the Editor role in new projects. When enabled, default service accounts in new projects have no access by default, requiring explicit role assignments that follow least privilege. Note that organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 have this constraint enforced by default. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts

column2: Your security team is deploying a new VPC Service Controls perimeter to protect sensitive BigQuery datasets. Before enforcing the perimeter in production, you need to verify that existing applications will continue to function correctly without blocking legitimate access. You want to minimize disruption while accurately identifying potential issues. What should you do?
column3: Configure the perimeter in dry run mode first and analyze the violation logs to identify applications that would be blocked before enforcing the perimeter.
column4: Deploy the perimeter directly in enforced mode and use the violation analyzer to troubleshoot any access denials that occur after deployment.
column5: Create the perimeter in enforced mode with all services unrestricted, then gradually add restricted services one at a time over several weeks.
column6: Configure access levels to allow all traffic initially, then remove access levels one by one to identify which applications require exceptions.
column8: Dry run mode logs violations as though the perimeters are enforced but does not prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to test perimeter configuration and identify potential issues before enforcing, minimizing disruption to existing applications. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: You are configuring Web Security Scanner to detect SQL injection and cross-site scripting vulnerabilities in a multi-project environment. The applications use non-standard ports for HTTPS connections. Some applications require authenticated scanning while others are public-facing. What configuration approach meets these requirements?
column3: Deploy a reverse proxy to redirect traffic from standard ports to non-standard ports, then use managed scans with organization-wide authentication.
