column4: Configure custom scans for each project, specify the non-standard port URLs as starting URLs, and configure authentication only for the applications that require it.
column5: Configure Security Command Center to aggregate custom scan findings across projects and use a single authentication profile for all applications.
column6: Enable managed scans at the organization level and configure port exceptions for non-standard HTTPS ports in the SCC settings.
column8: Custom scans support non-standard ports and can be configured per project with specific starting URLs. Custom scans also support authentication configuration for applications that require it, while public-facing applications can be scanned without authentication. This provides the flexibility needed for diverse application requirements. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-web-security-scanner-custom-scans

column2: Your security operations team needs to identify when log sources stop sending data to Google SecOps SIEM. You want to receive real-time alerts when critical data sources go silent. Which approach provides the most effective silent source detection with alerting capability?
column3: Configure Cloud Monitoring alerting policies using Chronicle Collector ingestion metrics with absence conditions to trigger notifications when log sources stop reporting.
column4: Use the Data Ingestion and Health dashboard's silent host monitoring widget to view hosts that have stopped reporting within the last 7 days.
column5: Configure the Data Health Monitoring and Troubleshooting dashboard to automatically send email notifications when irregularities are detected.
column6: Create a custom YARA-L rule that detects the absence of events from specific log types over a 24-hour window.
column8: Cloud Monitoring integration with Google SecOps allows you to create alerting policies based on ingestion metrics like Total ingested log count. Using absence conditions triggers alerts when collectors or log sources stop sending data within a defined threshold, providing real-time notification capability. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/ingestion/ingestion-notifications-for-health-metrics

column2: Your organization wants to detect when container images running in GKE clusters develop new vulnerabilities after deployment. You need to configure Binary Authorization to monitor for this condition and log violations without blocking existing workloads. What should you configure?
column3: Enable Binary Authorization enforcement with dry-run mode and review Cloud Audit Logs for images that would have been blocked due to missing attestations.
column4: Configure Artifact Analysis automatic scanning with notifications and create Cloud Monitoring alerts when new vulnerabilities are detected in images stored in Artifact Registry.
column5: Create a CV check-based platform policy with a vulnerability check that specifies maximum allowed severity levels, then enable CV on your clusters using the POLICY_BINDINGS evaluation mode.
column6: Configure a Cloud Function triggered by Artifact Analysis Pub/Sub notifications to cross-reference new vulnerability findings with GKE cluster deployments.
column8: The Binary Authorization Continuous Validation vulnerability check monitors for vulnerabilities in container images associated with running Pods. CV logs violations to Cloud Logging when vulnerabilities exceed configured thresholds. Using POLICY_BINDINGS mode enables CV monitoring without affecting Binary Authorization enforcement, allowing you to detect newly discovered vulnerabilities without blocking existing workloads. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/cv-vulnerability-check

column2: Your threat hunting team needs to detect potential lateral movement by identifying internal hosts that have recently started communicating with database servers they have never contacted before. You have 60 days of VPC Flow Logs in BigQuery. Which analytical approach best accomplishes this objective?
column3: Use BigQuery to identify new source-destination pairs in the last 24 hours that do not appear in the previous 59 days of historical data, filtering for destination IPs in database subnet ranges.
column4: Use BigQuery to count total connections per hour to database subnets and alert when the count exceeds the average by two standard deviations.
column5: Export the VPC Flow Logs to Google Security Operations and use built-in entity behavior analytics to automatically detect lateral movement without custom queries.
column6: Create scheduled queries in BigQuery that generate daily reports of all database connections sorted by bytes transferred and manually review for suspicious patterns.
column8: Detecting first-time connections to sensitive assets like databases is a key indicator of lateral movement or reconnaissance. Comparing recent connections against historical baselines identifies new communication patterns. This approach leverages the BigQuery capability to efficiently query large historical datasets for anomaly detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/architecture/security-log-analytics

column2: You are configuring a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to track security findings for multiple projects across your organization. You want analysts in a central security project to view aggregated security metrics from all monitored projects without requiring them to switch between projects. What should you configure?
column3: Enable cross-project dashboard sharing by granting the Monitoring Viewer role on all source projects and linking them through dashboard federation.
column4: Configure the metrics scope of the central security project to include all projects that should be monitored, and create dashboards in the central project.
column5: Create individual dashboards in each monitored project and use the Cloud Monitoring API to aggregate them into a single view in the central project.
column6: Export all project metrics to BigQuery and create a Looker Studio dashboard that queries the centralized BigQuery dataset.
column8: A metrics scope determines which projects' metric data is visible to a Google Cloud project. By configuring the metrics scope of the central security project to include all monitored projects, dashboards created in that project can display aggregated metric data from multiple projects without analysts needing to switch contexts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/settings#create-multi

column2: Your security team has detected potential lateral movement activity in your Google Cloud environment. You need to analyze VPC Flow Logs exported to BigQuery to identify a single internal VM that is connecting to an unusually high number of unique destination ports on other internal VMs within a 15-minute window. Which BigQuery SQL query pattern is most effective for detecting this port scanning behavior?
column3: Query VPC Flow Logs grouping by source and destination IP pairs and calculating average round-trip time, filtering for connections with latency anomalies.
column4: Query VPC Flow Logs grouping by source IP and counting distinct destination ports, filtering for internal-to-internal traffic, and applying a threshold for unique port count within the time window.
column5: Query VPC Flow Logs grouping by protocol number and counting packets, filtering for non-standard protocols that indicate malicious tunneling activity.
column6: Query VPC Flow Logs grouping by destination IP and summing total bytes transferred, filtering for the top ten talkers by bandwidth consumption within the time window.
column8: Port scanning for lateral movement is characterized by a single source connecting to many destination ports. Grouping by source IP and counting distinct destination ports allows identification of hosts exhibiting this scanning behavior. Filtering for internal traffic focuses on lateral movement within the VPC rather than external reconnaissance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/flow-logs

column2: Your security team monitors multiple services including a SIEM log collector, a threat intelligence feed processor, and a vulnerability scanner. Each service has defined SLOs. The security operations manager requests a unified dashboard showing the SLO status of all security services. You need to implement this while ensuring the dashboard reflects current SLO compliance. What should you do?
column3: Configure per-service dashboards in Cloud Monitoring and use the microservice dashboard feature to view individual service SLO status on separate pages.
column4: Create a custom dashboard and add multiple SLO widgets, with each widget configured to display the compliance or error budget status for each security service.
column5: Build individual alerting policy charts for each service and group them in a collapsible section on a custom dashboard.
column6: Export SLO metrics from all services to a centralized BigQuery dataset and create a Looker Studio report with scheduled daily updates.
column8: Custom dashboards can include multiple SLO widgets, each showing health, compliance, or error budget for different services. This provides a unified view of all security service SLOs in a single dashboard. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/dashboards/slos

column2: You need to create a YARA-L detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) that identifies when a user logs in from more than two different cities within a 10-minute time window. Which YARA-L rule structure correctly implements this detection?
column3: Create a single-event rule that uses a regex pattern to extract multiple cities from each login event.
column4: Use the match section to correlate events by user over 10m and add a condition that checks #city > 2 to count distinct city values.
column5: Write separate rules for each city pair combination and use composite detection to correlate them.
column6: Use the outcome section with an array function to store all login cities and trigger when the array exceeds two elements.
column8: The match section with a time window enables correlation of multiple events over a specified period. Using a placeholder variable for city and the condition '#city > 2' counts distinct values. This multi-event rule structure is the correct approach for detecting login anomalies across locations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-overview

column2: You are building a Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR playbook that needs to execute response actions on endpoints located in an isolated network segment that cannot be reached directly from the cloud platform. What should you implement to enable the playbook to communicate with these endpoints?
column3: Store playbook outputs in Cloud Storage and configure a scheduled task in the isolated network to poll for new commands.
column4: Configure VPN connectivity between Google SecOps and the isolated network segment to enable direct API communication.
column5: Create a webhook endpoint in the isolated network that receives playbook commands and executes them locally using custom scripts.
column6: Deploy a Remote Agent on a server within the isolated network and configure integrations to run actions remotely through the agent.
column8: The Remote Agent securely connects a cloud Google SecOps instance to remote sites, enabling execution of actions and playbooks on environments that cannot be directly accessed from the cloud. The agent communicates with Google SecOps through the Publisher proxy server. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/working-with-remote-agents/what-is-a-remote-agent

column2: You are configuring VPC Flow Logs for a subnet containing sensitive database servers to support threat hunting activities. The security team requires comprehensive visibility into connection attempts while managing storage costs. Which configuration balances security visibility requirements with cost optimization for detecting lateral movement threats?
column3: Set the aggregation interval to 5 seconds with a secondary sampling rate of 10% and include only base fields without metadata annotations.
column4: Set the aggregation interval to 15 minutes with a secondary sampling rate of 100% and exclude all metadata to minimize storage costs.
column5: Set the aggregation interval to 5 seconds with a secondary sampling rate of 50% and include all metadata annotations for maximum context.
column6: Set the aggregation interval to 10 minutes with a secondary sampling rate of 100% and filter to only capture traffic on ports 22 and 443.
column8: A 5-second aggregation interval provides granular visibility into rapid connection attempts typical of lateral movement and scanning, while 50% secondary sampling reduces log volume and costs. Including all metadata annotations provides essential context like source and destination VPC, instance, and project information needed for threat investigation and correlation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-flow-logs

column2: Your security operations team needs to create executive dashboards that visualize historical incident trends, including mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to remediate (MTTR), from Google Security Operations (SecOps) data. The dashboards must be shareable with stakeholders who do not have access to the SecOps platform. What should you do?
column3: Export Google SecOps data to BigQuery and connect Looker Studio to the BigQuery dataset to create interactive dashboards.
column4: Use the built-in SOAR advanced reports with Looker Explores and export individual report PDFs to stakeholders on a scheduled basis.
column5: Create scheduled queries in BigQuery that compute incident metrics and email the query results to stakeholders daily using Cloud Functions.
column6: Configure Google SecOps to stream detections directly to Looker Studio using the BigQuery connector without intermediate storage.
column8: Google SecOps can export data including rule detections, IOC matches, and UDM events to BigQuery. Looker Studio can then connect directly to BigQuery tables and views, allowing you to create interactive visualizations and share them with stakeholders without requiring SecOps platform access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: Your security team has completed a major incident investigation in Google Security Operations (SecOps) and needs to document the case resolution details for compliance reporting. Leadership requires a quarterly report showing incident trends, case closure rates, and mean time to remediate (MTTR). You need to design a sustainable solution using Google Cloud tools. What should you do?
column3: Use the built-in SOAR Dashboards widgets to track SOC metrics and manually export PDF screenshots quarterly for leadership review.
column4: Create custom YARA-L rules to aggregate case resolution statistics and output them to the Detection Engine for automated reporting.
column5: Export Google SecOps data to BigQuery and connect Looker Studio to create interactive dashboards that visualize case metrics and incident trends over time.
column6: Configure Cloud Logging to export all SecOps audit logs directly to a Cloud Storage bucket and use Google Sheets for analysis.
column8: Google SecOps provides managed data export to BigQuery that includes rule detections, UDM events, and ingestion metrics. Looker Studio (or other BI tools) can connect to BigQuery to create customizable dashboards and reports for compliance reporting. This approach supports long-term trend analysis and stakeholder communication. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: Your organization recently enabled curated detection rule sets in Google SecOps and wants to monitor which rules are generating detections, track detection trends over time, and understand which MITRE ATT&CK techniques are being detected. Which dashboard configuration provides the most comprehensive view?
column3: Navigate to the Main dashboard and review the Alerts total count and Global Threat Map visualization for IoC-based detection activity.
column4: Use the Curated Detections dashboard to view rule sets with detection activity, charts tracking rule activity over time, and MITRE technique mappings for each rule.
column5: Configure the Cloud Detection and Response dashboard with GCP Log Type filters to view CDIR alerts and data source coverage percentages.
column6: Create a custom dashboard using the Rule Detections Explore with detection count measures grouped by rule_name and severity dimensions.
column8: The Curated Detections dashboard displays information about each curated detection rule that generated detections, grouped by rule set. It includes charts tracking activity for each rule, detection counts, and MITRE ATT&CK technique mappings — providing comprehensive visibility into detection effectiveness. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/curated-detections

column2: Your organization has integrated Jira with Security Command Center Enterprise for case management. Security analysts report that tickets are not being created for threat detection findings generated by Event Threat Detection. You need to configure the system to create Jira tickets for threat cases. What should you do?
column3: Customize the threat response playbooks by adding a Jira ticket creation action, or create new playbooks specifically for threat cases.
column4: Update the Jira integration credentials in the SOAR Settings to enable automatic ticket creation for all finding types.
column5: Enable the Posture Findings With Jira playbook and configure it to include Event Threat Detection findings in its scope.
column6: Reconfigure the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector to include threat findings in its ingestion scope.
column8: By default, cases containing threat findings have no related tickets even when a ticketing system is integrated with Security Command Center Enterprise. To use tickets for threat cases, you must customize available playbooks by adding an action or create new playbooks that include ticket creation steps. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/cases-overview

column2: Your organization created an aggregated sink at the organization level to route Admin Activity audit logs to a Cloud Storage bucket. After verifying the sink configuration, you notice that log entries are arriving with a consistent delay of several hours. You need to understand this behavior to set appropriate expectations with stakeholders. What explains this delay?
column3: The Log Router's temporary buffer is full, causing a backlog in log delivery to the Cloud Storage destination.
column4: The organization-level aggregated sink has additional processing overhead that causes delays compared to project-level sinks.
column5: Routed log entries are saved to Cloud Storage buckets in hourly batches, and it typically takes 2 to 3 hours before entries appear at the destination.
column6: Cloud Storage requires time to index incoming log files before they become visible in the bucket.
column8: Cloud Logging sinks that route to Cloud Storage process logs in hourly batches. This batching behavior means logs are not written in real-time and there is an inherent delay of 2-3 hours before log entries appear in the Cloud Storage destination. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/storage

column2: Platform operations"Your organization has a folder structure where a production folder and a development folder exist under the organization node. A list-based organization policy constraint denies values 'X' and 'Y' at the organization level. The development folder needs to also deny value 'Z' while maintaining the denials inherited from the organization. How should you configure the organization policy on the development folder?
column3: Create an organization policy on the development folder that sets inheritFromParent to FALSE and specifies 'X', 'Y', and 'Z' in the deniedValues list.
column4: Apply the restoreDefault value at the development folder level and create a new policy that denies all three values.
column5: Delete the organization-level policy and create separate policies on both folders with their specific denied values.
column6: Create an organization policy on the development folder that sets inheritFromParent to TRUE and adds 'Z' to the deniedValues list.
column8: Setting inheritFromParent to TRUE merges the parent policy with the child policy. The effective policy will deny values 'X', 'Y' (inherited from the organization), and 'Z' (added at the folder level). This properly maintains the inherited denials while extending them. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/understanding-hierarchy

column2: During an incident investigation, you discover that a service account key has been compromised. The compromised service account was used to generate short-lived credentials through the Service Account Credentials API. You need to immediately revoke all access associated with this compromised credential. What should you do?
column3: Create an IAM deny policy for the service account to block all permissions and rotate the service account key.
column4: Disable or delete the compromised service account to immediately revoke both the service account key and any short-lived credentials.
column5: Delete the compromised service account key and wait for all short-lived credentials to expire naturally.
column6: Disable the compromised service account key using the IAM API and create a new key for legitimate workloads.
column8: Deleting a service account key alone does not revoke short-lived credentials that were issued based on the key. To revoke compromised short-lived credentials, you must disable or delete the service account itself. This immediately terminates all access for any workload using that service account. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/docs/security/compromised-credentials

column2: During a threat hunting exercise in Google Security Operations (SecOps), you identified a suspicious file hash that may be related to an ongoing campaign. You need to discover all related IOCs including associated domains, IP addresses, and URLs that share relationships with this hash. Which VirusTotal v3 integration actions should you use to expand your investigation?
column3: Use the Search IOCs action with the hash as a parameter to find all related indicators in the VirusTotal dataset.
column4: Use the Enrich Hash action to automatically retrieve all related IOCs including domains, IPs, and URLs in a single enrichment call.
column5: Use the Search Entity Graphs action to visualize and export all related IOCs from the hash's relationship graph.
column6: Use the Get Related Domains, Get Related IPs, and Get Related URLs actions to obtain all IOCs that have relationships with the file hash.
column8: The VirusTotal v3 integration provides specific actions - Get Related Domains, Get Related IPs, and Get Related URLs - designed to obtain related IOCs from a starting indicator such as a file hash. These actions require VirusTotal Enterprise (VTE) and support MD5, SHA-1, and SHA-256 hashes for pivoting to discover related infrastructure and indicators. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/marketplace-integrations/virustotal-v3

column2: Threat hunting"Your security team uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) with BigQuery data export enabled. You need to identify all historical IOC matches from the last 90 days to investigate potential compromises. Which BigQuery table should you query?
column3: The ioc_matches table, which stores IOC matches found against UDM events.
column4: The entity_graph table, which stores entity relationships and threat intelligence associations.
column5: The rule_detections table, which stores detections returned by YARA-L rules.
column6: The udm_events table with a filter for events containing threat intelligence indicators.
column8: Google SecOps exports IOC matches to the ioc_matches table in BigQuery. This table stores artifacts such as domains and IP addresses from events that match Indicator of Compromise feeds, making it the appropriate table for querying historical IOC matches. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: You need to create a log-based metric that extracts API response latency values from application logs to identify anomalous performance that may indicate a security incident. The logs contain a JSON field with latency in milliseconds. Which type of log-based metric should you create?
column3: A counter log-based metric with labels that extract the latency value for each unique response time.
column4: A boolean log-based metric that evaluates whether latency exceeds a specified threshold value.
column5: A system-defined log-based metric that tracks byte_count with a severity filter for error responses.
column6: A distribution log-based metric with a value extractor configured to capture the latency field from the JSON payload.
column8: Distribution metrics accumulate numeric data extracted from log entries and are specifically designed for tracking values like latency. Distribution metrics record the count, mean, sum of squared deviations, and histogram buckets of extracted values, enabling analysis of latency patterns and identification of anomalies. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/distribution-metrics

column2: Your organization wants to build real-time security dashboards in Looker Studio that display Security Command Center (SCC) findings. The dashboards must support historical trend analysis and allow stakeholders to drill down into specific finding categories and severities. You need to design the most effective data pipeline architecture. What should you do?
column3: Configure SCC continuous export to stream findings to BigQuery, then connect Looker Studio to the BigQuery dataset using the BigQuery connector.
column4: Configure SCC Pub/Sub notifications and create a Cloud Function to write findings directly to Looker Studio data sources.
column5: Use the SCC API to query findings directly from Looker Studio using a custom connector with OAuth authentication.
column6: Export SCC findings to Cloud Storage in JSON format, then import the files into Looker Studio using the file upload connector.
column8: SCC continuous export streams new and updated findings to BigQuery in near real-time. This feature is the recommended way to export Security Command Center findings to BigQuery because it is fully managed and creates a findings table clustered by source_id, finding_id, and event_time. Looker Studio can then connect directly to this BigQuery dataset to create interactive dashboards with drill-down capabilities. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-analyze-findings-in-big-query

column2: Observability"Your security team needs to detect when log sources stop sending data to Google SecOps SIEM. You want to configure Cloud Monitoring to alert when a custom metric tracking log ingestion volume has no data for 15 minutes. Which alerting policy condition type should you use?
column3: Create a MetricThreshold condition with a static threshold of 0, a comparison of 'less than or equal to', and a retest window of 15 minutes to detect zero ingestion.
column4: Create a PromQL-based alerting policy using the absent() function with a 15-minute evaluation interval to detect missing metric data.
column5: Create a MetricAbsence condition that monitors the custom log ingestion metric and configure the trigger absence time to 15 minutes to alert when no data arrives.
column6: Create a forecasted metric-value alerting policy that predicts when log ingestion will drop to zero within a 15-minute forecast window.
column8: MetricAbsence conditions are designed to alert when monitored metrics stop receiving data for a specified duration. This is the appropriate approach for detecting silent log sources. The 15-minute trigger absence time aligns with the requirement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/metric-absence

column2: Your organization has integrated Security Command Center Enterprise with Jira for ticketing. Security analysts notice that posture finding cases are not automatically creating Jira tickets. You need to ensure that vulnerability and misconfiguration findings create tickets when cases are opened. What should you do?
column3: Run the Create SCC Enterprise Cloud Posture Ticket Type action manually on each existing case to establish the Jira integration.
column4: Update the SCC Enterprise - Cloud Orchestration and Remediation use case to the latest version, which automatically enables Jira integration.
column5: Disable the Posture Findings - Generic playbook and enable the Posture Findings With Jira playbook in the Security Operations console.
column6: Configure the SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector to use Jira API credentials for direct ticket creation.
column8: When integrating with Jira, you must enable the appropriate playbook for your ticketing system. The Posture Findings With Jira playbook handles the synchronization between cases and Jira issues. The generic playbook must be disabled to avoid conflicts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/integrate-ticketing-systems

column2: Your organization has enabled Container Threat Detection for GKE clusters running on Container-Optimized OS. After several weeks, you notice that Container Threat Detection findings are missing container-specific information such as container name and pod name. You need to determine the root cause of this issue. What is the most likely explanation?
column3: Container Threat Detection is deployed in a VPC Service Controls perimeter that blocks communication with the metadata service.
column4: The Container Threat Detection service agent lacks the Container Threat Detection Service Agent IAM role required to access container metadata.
column5: The Kubernetes API server and container runtime are failing to deliver container information to the Container Threat Detection DaemonSet in time before findings are reported.
column6: The GKE clusters are running on a version that does not support Container Threat Detection's container metadata collection feature.
column8: Container Threat Detection passes container information through a user mode DaemonSet in a best-effort manner. Container information can be dropped from reported findings if Kubernetes and the container runtime fail to deliver the corresponding container information in time. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: You are designing a threat detection solution that uses BigQuery to correlate Cloud Logging data with threat intelligence indicators. Your organization generates approximately 50 TB of logs daily and requires cost-effective queries that can efficiently scan specific time ranges. Which table configuration should you use when creating the log sink to BigQuery?
column3: Configure the log sink to route logs to a single non-partitioned table with clustering on the timestamp column for faster queries.
column4: Configure the log sink to use date-sharded tables to separate logs into daily tables for easier management.
column5: Store logs in a log bucket with Log Analytics enabled, then create a linked BigQuery dataset to avoid partitioning configuration.
column6: Configure the log sink to use partitioned tables, partitioning by the timestamp column to enable partition pruning for time-range queries.
column8: Partitioned tables allow BigQuery to scan only the partitions that match the filter, significantly reducing the bytes read and query costs. For time-series log data, partitioning by timestamp enables efficient time-range queries through partition pruning, which is essential for large-scale log analysis. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/partitioned-tables

column2: Your organization is building a forensic investigation playbook in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR. During incident response, you need to preserve forensic artifacts by copying disk snapshots and log exports to a dedicated Cloud Storage bucket. The evidence must remain immutable throughout the investigation and potential legal proceedings. What should you configure on the forensic evidence bucket?
column3: Apply a retention policy without locking it and rely on IAM permissions to restrict delete operations from non-forensic accounts.
column4: Enable Object Versioning on the bucket and create a lifecycle rule to archive older versions to Coldline storage after 30 days.
column5: Set a retention policy on the bucket and lock it using Bucket Lock to prevent deletion or modification of evidence until the retention period expires.
column6: Configure Dual-region storage with automatic failover to ensure evidence availability across multiple geographic locations.
column8: Bucket Lock with a locked retention policy provides WORM (write-once-read-many) storage that prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten until the retention period expires. This is essential for maintaining chain of custody and meeting regulatory requirements for evidence preservation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: While threat hunting in your GKE environment, you discover a Container Threat Detection finding indicating that a suspicious binary was executed that was not part of the original container image. You need to collect evidence from the affected container before remediation. What is the recommended approach?
column3: Take a disk snapshot of the GKE node VM and create a forensic copy before any investigation to preserve the complete node state.
column4: Immediately delete the affected pod to prevent further damage, then review the Container Threat Detection findings in Security Command Center for forensic details.
column5: Export the Container Threat Detection finding to Cloud Logging and use Log Analytics to query for all processes executed in the affected container.
column6: Use kubectl exec to connect to the container environment and use kubectl cp to copy the suspicious binary to local storage for forensic analysis before stopping the container.
column8: If the container is still running, you can investigate the container environment directly using kubectl exec to connect to the container and kubectl cp to retrieve suspicious artifacts. This allows you to preserve evidence before remediation actions that would destroy the container state. The finding provides Pod_Name, Container_Name, and Pod_Namespace needed for these commands. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/findings/threats/piped-encoded-download

column2: Your organization requires real-time notifications when Event Threat Detection identifies high-severity threats in your Google Cloud environment. You need to send these alerts to your third-party SIEM system. Security Command Center Premium tier is activated at the organization level. What should you configure?
column3: Enable the Event Threat Detection API and configure your SIEM to poll the findings.list API endpoint every 60 seconds for new high-severity findings.
column4: Create a continuous export to Pub/Sub with a filter for high-severity Event Threat Detection findings, then configure your SIEM to subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic.
column5: Configure Cloud Logging to export Event Threat Detection findings directly to your SIEM using a log router sink with severity filters.
column6: Create a Cloud Run function that runs on a schedule to query Event Threat Detection findings and forward high-severity alerts to your SIEM.
column8: Continuous exports allow you to filter findings by severity and source, automatically publishing new findings to Pub/Sub in near-real time. Your SIEM can then subscribe to this topic to receive alerts. This is the recommended approach for organization-level SCC activations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-export-data

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise and you notice that Security Health Analytics is generating many findings that are being grouped into the same case. The security team wants to understand how case priority is determined when multiple findings with different severities are grouped together. How does Security Command Center Enterprise determine case priority?
column3: Case priority is calculated as a weighted average of all active finding severities, excluding muted findings from the calculation.
column4: Case priority is based on the highest finding severity among all findings in the case, including muted findings.
column5: Case priority is manually assigned by the case assignee based on their assessment of the overall risk of the grouped findings.
column6: Case priority defaults to the severity of the first finding ingested into the case and remains unchanged as new findings are added.
column8: Security Command Center automatically sets case priority based on the highest severity property among all findings in a case. Even if a finding is muted, if it has the highest severity, it defines the case priority. This ensures critical issues receive appropriate attention even when some findings are suppressed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/cases-overview

column2: Your security team needs to correlate firewall logs from Cloud Logging with a threat intelligence feed containing known malicious IP addresses stored in a separate BigQuery table. You want to implement a detection mechanism that identifies connections to malicious IPs at scale with efficient query performance. What should you do?
column3: Enable Cloud IDS to automatically match firewall traffic against the external threat intelligence feed without using BigQuery.
column4: Configure a log sink to route firewall logs to a BigQuery partitioned table, then create scheduled queries that use SQL JOINs to correlate the logs with the threat intelligence table.
column5: Use Log Analytics to query firewall logs, then manually export results to BigQuery for comparison with the threat intelligence table on a weekly basis.
column6: Configure a log sink to route firewall logs to Cloud Storage, then use Cloud Functions to parse logs and check each entry against the threat intelligence feed in real-time.
column8: Routing logs to a BigQuery partitioned table enables efficient SQL-based analysis at scale. Partitioned tables improve query performance by reducing bytes scanned through partition pruning. Scheduled queries with JOINs allow regular correlation between log data and the threat intelligence table, enabling detection of connections to known malicious IPs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/bigquery

column2: Your team has deployed a Cloud Function that automatically remediates Security Command Center findings. After deployment, you notice that some findings are being processed multiple times, causing redundant remediation attempts. What is the most likely cause and how should you address it?
column3: Configure the Cloud Function to update the finding state to INACTIVE after successful remediation and modify the NotificationConfig filter to exclude INACTIVE findings.
column4: Create a Cloud Spanner database to track processed finding IDs and implement deduplication logic in the Cloud Function before performing remediation.
column5: Enable exactly-once delivery on the Pub/Sub subscription to guarantee that each finding notification is processed only once by the Cloud Function.
column6: Increase the Pub/Sub message acknowledgment deadline to prevent message redelivery before the Cloud Function completes processing.
column8: When a finding is remediated, its state should be updated to INACTIVE in Security Command Center. If the NotificationConfig filter includes state = 'ACTIVE', updating the finding state prevents reprocessing. This ensures idempotent behavior and eliminates redundant remediation attempts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-api-manage-notifications

column2: Your incident response team is investigating a suspected container escape attack on a GKE node. Binary Authorization continuous validation (CV) detected that a pod is running an image from an untrusted directory. You need to determine whether the image was legitimately deployed with an override or if it represents a potential compromise. Which log query provides the most relevant forensic information?
column3: Query Binary Authorization CV logs with filter logName containing 'continuous_validation' to view the CV check failure details and determine if the image should have been blocked.
column4: Query Artifact Registry audit logs to determine when the untrusted image was pushed and by which identity to identify the potential attack origin.
column5: Query Cloud Audit Logs with filter resource.type='k8s_cluster' and protoPayload.methodName containing 'pods.create' and the specific image reference to identify deployment method and any breakglass or dry-run labels.
column6: Query Container Analysis API for attestation occurrences associated with the image digest to verify if proper attestations exist.
column8: Cloud Audit Logs for GKE clusters capture pod creation events with complete context including the deployment method, any Binary Authorization policy evaluation results, and labels indicating if breakglass or dry-run mode was used. This query reveals whether the untrusted image deployment was authorized or potentially malicious. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/viewing-audit-logs

column2: You are optimizing threat hunting operations in Google Security Operations (SecOps) and want to leverage the Google Threat Intelligence (GTI) score to prioritize IOC matches automatically. The GTI score system assigns numeric values to indicators based on their potential impact. Your team needs to understand how to interpret these scores for effective prioritization. Which statement accurately describes the GTI scoring system?
column3: GTI score is calculated from VirusTotal community voting data and determines the number of antivirus engine detections for an indicator.
column4: GTI score is a binary classification that marks indicators as either malicious or benign based on automated machine learning models.
column5: GTI score is a numeric value from 0-100 that represents an indicator's potential impact, combining Mandiant Threat Intelligence data with analyst expertise.
column6: GTI score is assigned manually by security analysts when reviewing IOC matches and ranges from Low to Critical severity.
column8: The GTI score system calculates threat levels for indicators including domains, IP addresses, file hashes, and URLs. The score is a numeric representation from 0-100 of an indicator's potential impact if detected in an environment, combining Mandiant Threat Intelligence data with analyst expertise. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/understand-ic-score

column2: Your organization is establishing a data classification baseline for Google Cloud assets. You need to configure Cloud Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to continuously monitor BigQuery tables across all projects in your organization and report sensitivity levels. The results must be integrated with Security Command Center (SCC) for centralized visibility. What should you do?
column3: Use the DLP API content.inspect method to scan each table synchronously and store results in a BigQuery dataset for SCC integration.
column4: Create individual inspection jobs for each BigQuery table and configure Pub/Sub notifications to forward results to Security Command Center.
column5: Configure Cloud Audit Logs for BigQuery data access and create a Cloud Function to call the DLP API for classification when tables are modified.
column6: Configure a discovery scan configuration at the organization level, select relevant infoTypes, and enable the Publish to Security Command Center action.
column8: The discovery service continuously monitors data resources across the organization, classifies data into infoTypes, and calculates sensitivity levels. Enabling the Publish to Security Command Center action allows the data profiles to appear as findings in SCC for centralized asset context enrichment and risk management. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/data-profiles

column2: Your security team needs to store Cloud Audit Logs in Cloud Storage for 7 years to meet regulatory compliance requirements. The logs must be immutable and cannot be deleted or modified before the retention period expires. Which Cloud Storage configuration should you implement?
column3: Configure Object Lifecycle Management to transition logs to Archive storage class after 90 days with a delete action after 7 years.
column4: Configure a retention policy on the Cloud Storage bucket with a 7-year retention period and lock the policy using Bucket Lock.
column5: Set IAM policies on the Cloud Storage bucket to deny the storage.objects.delete permission for all users for 7 years.
column6: Enable Object Versioning on the Cloud Storage bucket to preserve all historical versions of log files for 7 years.
column8: Bucket Lock with a locked retention policy provides WORM (Write Once Read Many) storage that prevents objects from being deleted or modified until the retention period expires. Locking the policy is an irreversible action that ensures compliance with regulatory requirements such as SEC 17a-4(f), CFTC, and FINRA. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: Your threat intelligence team has discovered new IOCs that may have been present in your environment before they were identified. You need to search for these IOCs across historical log data that was ingested into Google Security Operations (SecOps) over the past 30 days. You have already created a YARA-L detection rule that includes the IOCs in a reference list. What should you do?
column3: Enable the rule with alerting turned on and wait for the detection engine to automatically re-evaluate all historical data.
column4: Export all historical UDM events to BigQuery and run a SQL query that matches against the IOC reference list.
column5: Update the reference list with the new IOCs and the detection engine will automatically scan all retained historical logs.
column6: Execute a retrohunt for the rule specifying the 30-day historical time range to evaluate past events against the new detection logic.
column8: Retrohunts allow you to run a rule against historical data over a specified time range. This is the proper method to search for IOCs within previously ingested data and identify if threats existed before the rule was created. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization recently activated Security Command Center Premium tier and enabled Event Threat Detection. You want to detect network-based malware activity using domain resolution data. Some of your VPC networks have VPC Flow Logs disabled to manage logging costs. What should you do to enable malware detection while controlling costs?
column3: Enable VPC Flow Logs with a 1-second aggregation interval and 100% sample rate to ensure comprehensive malware detection coverage.
column4: Enable Cloud DNS logging for the VPC networks since Event Threat Detection can detect malware using domain resolution without requiring VPC Flow Logs.
column5: Create Event Threat Detection custom modules to detect malware patterns in Cloud Audit Logs since they are always enabled and free.
column6: Export all network logs to BigQuery and run Event Threat Detection queries against the exported data to detect malware activity.
column8: Event Threat Detection can detect malware using Cloud DNS logs through domain resolution. The documentation states that for most users, Cloud DNS logs are sufficient for network detection of malware. VPC Flow Logs provide additional visibility but incur costs, and Cloud DNS logging is a cost-effective alternative. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: You want to create a Cloud Monitoring dashboard that visualizes Security Command Center findings by severity level over time. The dashboard should display metrics derived from SCC findings logs that are routed to Cloud Logging. What should you do first?
column3: Create log-based metrics in Cloud Logging using filters for SCC findings, then add chart widgets to the dashboard that query these metrics.
column4: Import the SCC dashboard template from Cloud Monitoring's curated dashboard gallery and customize it.
column5: Configure Security Command Center to export findings directly to Cloud Monitoring using the built-in metrics integration.
column6: Create custom metrics using the Cloud Monitoring API that poll the Security Command Center API for finding counts.
column8: Log-based metrics allow you to derive Cloud Monitoring metrics from log entries. By creating log-based metrics filtered for SCC findings and grouped by severity, you can chart these metrics on custom dashboards to visualize finding trends over time. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics

column2: During an active security incident investigation, you discovered a new malicious IP address that was not previously in your threat intelligence feeds. You need to determine whether any assets in your environment have communicated with this IP address during the past 90 days. Which approach should you use in Google Security Operations (SecOps)?
column3: Execute a retrohunt using a YARA-L rule that matches network events containing the malicious IP address to search historical data.
column4: Use the Asset view to manually search each asset's timeline for connections to the IP address over the investigation period.
column5: Submit a request to Google Customer Care to add the IP address to the curated detection rule sets for future alerting.
column6: Configure a new Applied Threat Intelligence feed containing the IP address and wait for the system to automatically correlate matches.
column8: Retrohunts allow you to run detection rules against historical data in Google SecOps. With 12 months of hot data retention by default, you can search across 90 days of data to identify any past communications with the malicious IP address. This is the most effective approach for searching historical data with specific IOCs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization uses Cloud Identity to manage user identities and wants to detect potential privilege escalation attempts by monitoring when users are added to privileged Google Groups that have IAM role bindings. You want to create a baseline of normal group membership changes and alert on suspicious additions. Which log type should you prioritize for this detection use case?
column3: Access Transparency logs filtered for IAM policy modifications by Google personnel
column4: Google Workspace Login Audit logs filtered for authentication to privileged applications
column5: Cloud Audit Logs Data Access audit logs for the IAM API service
column6: Cloud Identity Admin audit logs filtered for Groups-related events showing membership modifications
column8: Admin audit logs track actions performed in the Google Admin Console, including when administrators add users to groups. Since Google Groups are the recommended way to grant access to Google Cloud resources through IAM policies, monitoring these logs for membership changes provides visibility into potential privilege escalation through group-based access control. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/logs-based-security-alerting-in-google-cloud

column2: Your organization is planning to deploy Event Threat Detection custom modules across a multi-tier Google Cloud environment. The security team needs to understand the quotas and limits that apply to custom module operations. Which statement accurately describes the limits for Event Threat Detection custom modules?
column3: Each project can have 50 custom modules, with inheritance from organization counting against the project quota and unlimited findings.
column4: Custom modules have no configuration size limits, but API calls are rate-limited to 100 requests per minute per project.
column5: Custom modules are unlimited, but findings are capped at 1000 per project per day to prevent alert fatigue.
column6: The default quota allows 200 custom modules per organization, 6 MB maximum size per module, and 200 findings per parent resource per hour.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules have specific limits: a default quota of 200 custom modules that can be created, a 6 MB size limit for each custom module's configuration, and a rate limit of 200 custom module findings per parent resource (organization or project) per hour. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your security team needs to automatically trigger threat hunting searches in Google Security Operations (SecOps) whenever Security Command Center (SCC) detects a new high-severity threat finding. You want to build an event-driven architecture that uses Cloud Functions with Pub/Sub. What is the first configuration step you should complete?
column3: Deploy a Cloud Function with an HTTP trigger that receives webhook calls directly from Security Command Center.
column4: Create a Cloud Function that polls the Security Command Center API every minute to check for new high-severity findings.
column5: Configure a Cloud Scheduler job to trigger a Cloud Function that queries SCC for findings on an hourly basis.
column6: Configure a continuous export in Security Command Center to send findings to a Pub/Sub topic, filtering for high-severity threat findings.
column8: SCC continuous exports allow automatic publishing of findings to Pub/Sub topics in near-real time, with filters to select specific finding types. This creates the event source that triggers downstream Cloud Functions for automated threat hunting. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-export-data

column2: Your organization uses Binary Authorization continuous validation (CV) with check-based platform policies on your GKE clusters. During a security review, you need to identify all running Pods whose container images no longer comply with the current security policy. The policy includes checks for trusted directories and image freshness. What should you do?
column3: Use kubectl to describe each Pod and verify that images have the required attestations by checking Pod annotations.
column4: Export the Binary Authorization policy and compare image digests of all running Pods against the requireAttestationsBy attestors.
column5: Enable Binary Authorization enforcement mode to automatically terminate Pods that violate the platform policy and review termination events.
column6: Query Cloud Logging using the filter logName:'binaryauthorization.googleapis.com/continuous_validation' to view CV policy violation logs for non-compliant Pods.
column8: Binary Authorization continuous validation (CV) periodically checks images associated with running Pods and logs violations to Cloud Logging. The log entries appear at the binaryauthorization.googleapis.com/continuous_validation path and include details about which checks failed, such as TrustedDirectoryCheck or image freshness violations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/quickstart-cv

column2: Security Command Center has detected a toxic combination finding in your production environment. The finding indicates a Compute Engine VM with a publicly accessible IP address has an unpatched critical CVE, and the VM has service account access to a Cloud Storage bucket containing customer data. You need to understand how to respond to this finding. What should you do?
column3: Review the toxic combination case in the Risk section, examine the attack path evidence, and prioritize remediation of the contributing findings to eliminate the attack path.
column4: Create a YARA-L rule in Google SecOps to correlate the individual findings and generate a custom alert for the combined risk scenario.
column5: Mute the toxic combination finding since it is a duplicate detection of individual vulnerabilities already tracked by Security Health Analytics.
column6: Disable the Risk Engine service to stop generating toxic combination findings and focus on individual vulnerability findings instead.
column8: Toxic combination findings identify when multiple security issues combine to create a significantly higher risk than any individual finding. Reviewing the case provides the attack path visualization and related findings, enabling you to understand and remediate the underlying issues that create the toxic combination. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/toxic-combinations-manage

column2: You are configuring a CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions that needs to deploy resources to Google Cloud. Following security best practices, you want to eliminate the use of service account keys. You have created a workload identity pool and provider for GitHub. When granting the Workload Identity User role on your deployment service account, which approach follows the principle of least privilege?
column3: Grant the role at the project level so all service accounts in the project can be impersonated by GitHub workflows.
column4: Grant the role to specific external identities using attribute conditions that match the GitHub repository and branch where deployments are authorized.
column5: Grant the role to all members of the workload identity pool to simplify management across multiple repositories.
column6: Create a service account key with a 90-day expiration and store it as a GitHub secret for improved security over permanent keys.
column8: Best practices recommend granting the Workload Identity User role to specific external identities or identities that match certain criteria, rather than to all members of a workload identity pool. Using attribute conditions to match specific repositories and branches ensures that only authorized GitHub Actions workflows can impersonate the service account. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-workload-identity-federation

column2: Your organization wants to use Web Security Scanner to detect SQL injection vulnerabilities in your GKE-deployed web application that connects to Cloud SQL. You need to configure scans that maximize vulnerability detection coverage while minimizing the risk of data modification in production. What risk level configuration should you use?
column3: Use managed scans instead of custom scans since managed scans automatically use safe read-only operations that cannot modify database records.
column4: Configure the custom scan with LOW risk level, which minimizes requests with the potential to modify data while still detecting SQL injection vulnerabilities.
column5: Configure custom scans with NORMAL risk level and add the database tables to an exclude list to prevent any modification attempts.
column6: Configure the custom scan with NORMAL risk level to achieve maximum scan coverage, since Web Security Scanner automatically prevents data modification during scans.
column8: The LOW risk level is specifically designed to minimize requests that could potentially modify data. This is appropriate for scanning production environments where data integrity is critical. SQL injection detection capabilities are maintained, but the scanner is more conservative in its testing approach. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/python/docs/reference/websecurityscanner/latest/google.cloud.websecurityscanner_v1.types.ScanConfig

column2: Your organization activated Security Command Center Premium at the organization level and enabled Event Threat Detection. You want to ensure your security operations team receives near-real-time notifications when high-severity threat findings are generated. The notifications should be sent to your existing SIEM system that can consume from Pub/Sub. What should you configure?
column3: Enable the SCC Enterprise tier and use Google Security Operations SOAR playbooks to send notifications to your external SIEM system.
column4: Create a continuous export to Pub/Sub with a filter for threat findings and high severity, then configure your SIEM to subscribe to the designated Pub/Sub topic.
column5: Configure Cloud Logging exports from Security Command Center to Cloud Logging, then create a log-based alert that forwards to Pub/Sub.
column6: Create a BigQuery export configuration with a filter for high-severity threats, then configure your SIEM to query BigQuery periodically.
column8: Continuous exports automatically export new findings to Pub/Sub in near-real time when they match the filter criteria. You can create a filter like severity='HIGH' AND findingClass='THREAT' to export only high-severity threat findings. Your SIEM can then subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic to ingest findings into your existing workflow. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-export-data

column2: Your compliance team requires that security logs stored in Cloud Storage cannot be deleted or modified for seven years to meet SEC regulations. You need to configure the Cloud Storage bucket that receives routed logs from Cloud Logging. What should you do?
column3: Configure Object Versioning on the bucket and set a lifecycle rule to delete versions after seven years.
column4: Set a lifecycle rule on the bucket that transitions objects to Archive storage after 30 days with a minimum retention period of seven years.
column5: Set a retention policy on the Cloud Storage bucket with a seven-year retention period and lock the retention policy.
column6: Create an organization policy constraint that restricts object deletion on the bucket for seven years.
column8: Bucket Lock lets you set a retention policy on a bucket that prevents objects from being deleted or modified until the retention period expires. Locking the policy makes it permanent and helps meet regulatory requirements like SEC compliance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: Your organization is implementing Security Command Center Enterprise and wants to automatically assign posture finding cases to the appropriate resource owners for remediation. You need to configure the system to determine resource ownership. What is the order of precedence that Security Command Center uses to determine the resource owner for posture findings?
column3: Cloud tags, then Essential Contacts, then the Fallback Owner parameter in the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector.
column4: The project owner IAM role, then folder-level security contacts, then organization administrators.
column5: The Fallback Owner parameter, then Cloud tags, then a random assignment from the Security Operations team.
column6: Essential Contacts, then Cloud tags, then the IAM principal who created the resource.
column8: Security Command Center determines resource ownership following this specific order of precedence. The connector first checks for cloud tags inherited from the resource, then Essential Contacts if no tags exist, and finally uses the Fallback Owner parameter as the default assignee if neither is available. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/determine-ownership-posture-findings

column2: Your organization has detected a compromised VM in a production VPC network. You need to design an incident containment playbook that immediately isolates the infected VM from the rest of the network while allowing forensic analysis from a dedicated security team. According to Google Cloud best practices, which approach should you implement in the containment playbook?
column3: Apply a network tag to the infected VM and create high-priority VPC firewall rules that deny all ingress and egress traffic except from the forensics team's subnet CIDR.
column4: Configure a new service account on the infected VM and use service account-based firewall rules to restrict traffic to forensics infrastructure only.
column5: Modify the VPC subnet's Private Google Access settings to prevent the infected VM from accessing any external resources or Google APIs.
column6: Create a new VPC Service Controls perimeter in enforced mode and move the infected project to isolate it from all Google Cloud managed services immediately.
column8: VPC firewall rules using network tags allow you to immediately isolate specific VMs by applying deny rules that block all traffic except from specified trusted sources. High-priority rules ensure these containment rules take precedence over existing allow rules. This approach enables forensic analysis while preventing lateral movement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls

column2: Your security team detected a potential data exfiltration incident involving a Cloud Storage bucket. You need to investigate what configuration changes were made to the bucket's IAM policy over the past two weeks to identify when unauthorized access was granted. What should you do?
column3: Navigate to the Security Command Center Assets page, select the bucket, and view the Change History tab to see IAM modifications.
column4: Use the Cloud Asset Inventory BatchGetAssetsHistory API with the IAM_POLICY content type to retrieve the bucket's IAM policy history for the specified time window.
column5: Query Cloud Audit Logs for SetIamPolicy operations on the bucket and reconstruct the policy change timeline manually.
column6: Export the current IAM policy using gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy and compare it against backup copies from your configuration management system.
column8: BatchGetAssetsHistory retrieves the change history for specified assets within a time window up to 35 days in the past. By specifying the IAM_POLICY content type, you can see all IAM policy versions and when changes occurred for the Cloud Storage bucket. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/get-asset-history

column2: Your security team is using Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR to manage incident response. Analysts report that playbooks are running to completion before manual approvals can be obtained from the security manager. You need to configure the playbook to pause and notify the appropriate person while waiting for approval. What should you do?
column3: Create a separate playbook block that sends an email to the security manager requesting approval before continuing.
column4: Configure the action's Action Type as Manual, assign it to a specific user or SOC role, and add a message explaining what needs to be done.
column5: Enable the Time to respond setting on the trigger to ensure analysts have time to review before the playbook starts.
column6: Add a conditional flow step that checks whether the security manager has responded in the past 24 hours before proceeding.
column8: When you set an action's Action Type to Manual and assign it to a user or SOC role, the playbook pauses execution at that step. The manual action appears in the Pending Actions widget, requiring the assignee to execute or skip the action before the playbook continues. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/assign-actions-and-playbook-blocks

column2: Your security operations center has received intelligence about a new threat campaign using specific domains for command and control communications. You need to configure Event Threat Detection to detect if any resources in your organization communicate with these malicious domains. The built-in Malware: Bad Domain detector does not recognize these newly identified domains. What is the most appropriate approach?
column3: Submit a feature request to Google to add the domains to the built-in threat intelligence database used by the Malware: Bad Domain detector.
column4: Configure VPC Service Controls to block all outbound traffic to the malicious domains and export the blocked connection logs to Security Command Center.
column5: Create a Configurable Bad IP custom module and add the resolved IP addresses of the malicious domains to the module configuration.
column6: Enable Cloud DNS logging across your organization and create a Configurable Bad Domain custom module with your threat intelligence domains to detect DNS queries.
column8: The Configurable Bad Domain custom module allows you to specify custom domain indicators that Event Threat Detection will use to generate findings when DNS queries match. Cloud DNS logging must be enabled for Event Threat Detection to analyze domain resolution activity and detect connections to the specified malicious domains. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your threat hunting team receives a new batch of high-confidence IOCs from Mandiant related to an active breach campaign. You need to determine if any of these IOCs have been seen in your environment over the past 90 days using Google SecOps. The team wants to use the most effective method for searching historical data. What should you do?
column3: Run a retrohunt using YARA-L rules that match the new IOCs against historical event data stored in Google SecOps.
column4: Create reference lists with the IOCs and configure the detection engine to generate alerts on all previously ingested events.
column5: Export all historical logs to BigQuery and run SQL queries matching the IOCs against the exported data.
column6: Enable Applied Threat Intelligence curated detections and wait for alerts to be generated based on the new IOCs.
column8: Retrohunt allows you to use rules to search for detections throughout existing historical data in Google SecOps. This is the most effective method for searching past events against newly discovered IOCs across a specified time period. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your security team is designing an incident response playbook to prevent data exfiltration from sensitive BigQuery datasets during a potential breach. You need to implement a containment mechanism that restricts which external resources can receive data from protected projects. Which VPC Service Controls configuration should you include in the playbook?
column3: Configure IAM deny policies on the BigQuery datasets to prevent any data export operations to external projects.
column4: Configure egress rules in the service perimeter to restrict which external projects, services, and identities can receive data from resources inside the perimeter.
column5: Create VPC firewall rules with destination IP ranges that block all egress traffic from VMs in the protected project to prevent BigQuery data exports.
column6: Enable VPC accessible services to restrict which services are available from network endpoints inside the perimeter.
column8: VPC Service Controls egress rules allow you to constrain the exact services, methods, Google Cloud projects, VPC networks, and identities that can access data outside the perimeter, minimizing exfiltration risk during an incident. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/ingress-egress-rules

column2: During a security incident investigation, you need to test new VPC Service Controls perimeter configurations to contain a potential threat without disrupting production workloads. You want to validate that the containment rules will block unauthorized access patterns observed in your logs while ensuring legitimate business processes continue functioning. What should you do?
column3: Deploy the new perimeter configuration using dry-run mode, analyze violation logs in BigQuery to validate effectiveness, then enforce the configuration once validated.
column4: Use the VPC Service Controls violation analyzer to retroactively assess how the new configuration would have affected historical access patterns.
column5: Deploy the perimeter in enforced mode during a maintenance window when traffic is minimal to reduce potential business impact.
column6: Create the perimeter in enforced mode on a test project, simulate attack patterns, then apply the same configuration to production projects.
column8: Dry-run mode logs violations without blocking access, allowing you to test containment configurations against live traffic patterns. You can export logs to BigQuery for analysis, verify that the configuration blocks the threat patterns while permitting legitimate access, then enforce once validated. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: Your organization recently activated Security Command Center Premium at the organization level. You want Event Threat Detection to detect malware-related threats by monitoring network connections to known malicious IP addresses. You have Cloud DNS logging enabled but need additional network visibility. What should you consider when enabling VPC Flow Logs for this purpose?
column3: Cloud DNS logs are required to enable VPC Flow Log analysis in Event Threat Detection, and both log types must be enabled simultaneously.
column4: VPC Flow Logs must be configured with a 1-second aggregation interval and 100% sample rate to ensure Event Threat Detection can detect all malware communications.
column5: Event Threat Detection requires VPC Flow Logs for all network-based threat detection and cannot detect malware using Cloud DNS logs alone.
column6: VPC Flow Logs can incur costs, so Google recommends increasing the aggregation interval to 15 minutes and reducing the sample rate to 5-10% to balance detection recall with cost management.
column8: While VPC Flow Logs provide additional network visibility beyond Cloud DNS logs for malware detection, they can incur costs. Google recommends increasing the aggregation interval to 15 minutes and reducing the sample rate to between 5% and 10% to manage costs, though there is a tradeoff between recall (higher sample rate) and cost management. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: You need to configure Security Command Center to automatically detect when resources in your environment communicate with malicious domains identified by your security research team. The solution must generate findings in SCC with custom descriptions and remediation steps. Which approach should you use?
column3: Enable the built-in Malware: Bad Domain Event Threat Detection detector and upload your domains list to Google Threat Intelligence for automatic detection.
column4: Export Cloud DNS logs to BigQuery and create scheduled queries that match DNS requests against your malicious domains list, then use Cloud Functions to create SCC findings.
column5: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module using the CONFIGURABLE_BAD_DOMAIN module type, specifying your domains list and configuring custom metadata including description and recommendation fields.
column6: Configure Cloud Armor security policies with custom rules to block traffic to malicious domains and enable logging to generate findings in Security Command Center.
column8: Event Threat Detection provides the CONFIGURABLE_BAD_DOMAIN custom module type that allows you to configure detection for connections to specific domains you maintain. The module template lets you define custom metadata including severity, description, and remediation recommendations that appear in the generated findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-etd-overview

column2: Your organization has multiple applications deployed on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that access various Google Cloud APIs. The security team has raised concerns about over-permissioning in the current configuration where all applications share a single service account with broad permissions. You want to implement least privilege access while using Workload Identity Federation for GKE. What should you do?
column3: Create a single service account with fine-grained IAM conditions that restrict access based on the requesting Pod's namespace and service account name.
column4: Grant each GKE namespace the Workload Identity User role on all service accounts and let administrators manage access at the namespace level only.
column5: Use the default Compute Engine service account for all workloads and configure access scopes to restrict API access for each application.
column6: Create dedicated service accounts for each application and grant each service account only the specific IAM roles needed for that application's API access.
column8: Best practices recommend creating dedicated service accounts for each application. Using application-specific service accounts helps avoid over-permissioning by only granting access to resources that each individual application requires. This follows the principle of least privilege and enables better auditability. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-workload-identity-federation

column2: Your organization has deployed Security Command Center Enterprise and wants to implement case management for toxic combination findings. You need to configure the system to automatically create and manage cases for these high-risk findings. What is required to enable toxic combination case management?
column3: Configure the Google Chronicle - Chronicle Alerts Connector to ingest toxic combination findings and manually create playbook triggers.
column4: Install the SCC Enterprise - Cloud Orchestration and Remediation use case version dated June 25, 2024 or later from the Security Operations console Marketplace.
column5: Create custom YARA-L rules in Google SecOps to detect toxic combination patterns and configure alert-to-case mappings.
column6: Enable the toxic combination detection module in Security Health Analytics settings and configure a custom Pub/Sub notification channel.
column8: The toxic combination feature requires the June 25, 2024 or later release of the SCC Enterprise - Cloud Orchestration and Remediation use case. This use case introduces widgets, playbooks, and enhancements to support the management of toxic combination findings and cases in the Security Operations console. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/toxic-combinations-manage

column2: Your SOC team has developed a common notification and approval workflow that multiple playbooks need to incorporate. The workflow includes sending emails, requesting manager approval, and changing case stages. Team members frequently update this workflow to improve response times. You want to ensure all playbooks using this workflow benefit from updates automatically. What should you implement in Google SecOps SOAR?
column3: Create a custom integration in the IDE that encapsulates the entire workflow as a single action.
