column4: Create a standalone playbook and manually copy its steps into each parent playbook that requires it.
column5: Create a playbook block with input parameters for the workflow and insert it into parent playbooks.
column6: Export the workflow as a use case and import it separately into each environment.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks that implement common workflows across multiple playbooks. Any edit to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it, which meets the requirement for automatic updates. Blocks can accept input parameters to adjust their behavior when used in different contexts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Your organization operates a security API gateway that handles authentication and authorization requests from multiple applications. You need to create an SLO in Cloud Monitoring to track the latency performance of your security service. The SLI requires measuring the 95th percentile latency to ensure it remains below 100 milliseconds for at least 99% of measurement windows over a 28-day period. Which SLO type should you use?
column3: A request-based SLO using TimeSeriesRatio to calculate the ratio of fast requests to total requests.
column4: A request-based SLO using a DistributionCut structure to measure the fraction of requests completing under 100 milliseconds.
column5: A windows-based SLO because the raw metric is a latency percentile that requires measuring goodness over discrete time windows.
column6: A request-based SLO configured with GAUGE metric kind to track instantaneous latency values.
column8: Windows-based SLOs are required when the raw metric is a latency percentile. This approach measures the number of time windows where the 95th percentile latency meets the threshold, then calculates compliance as the fraction of good windows to total windows. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring/sli-metrics/lb-metrics

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Enterprise tier and needs to prioritize remediation of vulnerability findings that pose the highest risk to your critical production systems. The security team wants to focus on vulnerabilities that provide potential attackers with the easiest path to your high-value resources. Which SCC capability should you use to prioritize remediation?
column3: Create custom compliance standards in SCC and prioritize vulnerabilities based on the number of compliance violations associated with each finding.
column4: Filter vulnerability findings by severity classification and prioritize CRITICAL severity findings over HIGH severity findings for immediate remediation.
column5: Use attack exposure scores calculated by the Risk Engine to prioritize findings that expose high-value resources, then sort findings by score on the Findings page.
column6: Use the CVSS base scores from vulnerability findings to prioritize remediation, focusing on findings with CVSS scores above 9.0.
column8: Attack exposure scores are dynamic indicators calculated after findings are generated. The score is specific to each finding instance and is based on factors including which resource instances are affected and the difficulty an attacker would face reaching high-value resources. You can sort findings by attack exposure score on the Findings page to identify the highest-risk vulnerabilities. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/vulnerabilities-prioritize-remediation

column2: During an incident investigation, you suspect that a compromised service account may have been used to access resources across multiple projects in your organization. You want to determine all IAM role bindings that grant this service account access to any resources within your organization's scope. Which approach should you use?
column3: Use the IAM Troubleshooter to check if the service account has access to each resource individually across all projects.
column4: Query Cloud Audit Logs for all protoPayload.serviceName='iam.googleapis.com' entries containing the service account email.
column5: Use IAM Policy Analyzer with the service account email as the principal parameter and scope the query to the organization.
column6: Export all project-level IAM policies to BigQuery and run SQL queries to search for the service account in member fields.
column8: IAM Policy Analyzer lets you query for all IAM role bindings that match specific criteria. By specifying the service account as the principal and setting the organization as the scope, it will analyze allow policies attached to the organization and all descendant resources to find where the service account has access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/analyze-iam-policies

column2: Your security team has identified a new threat campaign affecting your industry. You have a list of file hashes associated with this campaign and want to determine whether any of these IOCs have appeared in your Google Security Operations (SecOps) environment over the past 90 days. You want to use the most efficient method to correlate these IOCs with historical event data. What should you do?
column3: Create a YARA-L detection rule matching the file hashes and run a retrohunt against the historical data.
column4: Enable Applied Threat Intelligence and wait for automatic IOC matching to occur.
column5: Export your logs to BigQuery and use SQL queries with the file hash list to search historical data.
column6: Configure the VirusTotal v3 integration Search IOCs action to query each hash against your SIEM data.
column8: A retrohunt allows you to run a YARA-L rule against existing historical data in Google SecOps to search for detections throughout that data. By creating a rule that matches the known malicious file hashes and executing a retrohunt, you can efficiently identify if any of these IOCs appeared in your environment over the past 90 days. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your security team has enabled Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) curated detections in Google Security Operations (SecOps). You notice that analysts are receiving a high volume of alerts for medium-priority IOC matches but want them to focus primarily on active breach and high-priority indicators. What should you do to optimize alert prioritization?
column3: Configure the IOC matches page filter to only display Active Breach and High priority IOCs and train analysts to use this view.
column4: Disable the Medium Priority Host Indicators and Medium Priority Network Indicators rule sets while keeping Active Breach and High Priority rule sets enabled.
column5: Create a suppression rule to filter out all IOC matches that have a GTI score below 80.
column6: Modify the ATI detection rules to change the priority threshold from medium to high in the rule conditions.
column8: ATI curated detections include separate rule sets for different priority levels including Active Breach, High, and Medium. You can selectively enable or disable individual rule sets to focus analyst attention on the most critical indicators. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-curated-detections

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR to automate phishing investigations. You need to configure a playbook that triggers only when an alert contains the word 'malware activity' in the alert name. Which trigger type should you use in the playbook?
column3: All trigger to capture every alert and add a conditional flow step to filter for 'malware activity'.
column4: Alert Type trigger configured with the value 'malware activity'.
column5: Product Name trigger with 'malware activity' as the product identifier.
column6: Custom Trigger with a placeholder condition matching 'malware activity' in the alert name field.
column8: Custom Trigger allows you to define custom placeholders for highly specific matches, such as checking if the alert name includes specific text like 'malware activity'. This provides the most precise control for conditional triggering based on alert field values. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-triggers-in-playbooks

column2: Your organization has deployed Event Threat Detection custom modules at the organization level to detect connections to suspicious IP addresses. A development project team wants to disable one specific inherited custom module for their project without affecting other projects. What should the project team do?
column3: Clone the organization-level custom module to the project level and configure it with different detection parameters.
column4: Delete the custom module at the organization level and recreate it with an exclusion for the development project.
column5: Submit a request to Cloud Customer Care to add the development project to an exclusion list for the custom module.
column6: Update the inherited custom module's enablement state to DISABLED at the project level using the Google Cloud console or gcloud CLI.
column8: When you enable or disable an inherited custom module, your changes are only applied to your current resource level. The original custom module residing at the parent level is not affected. This allows the project team to disable the module for their project while other projects continue to inherit the enabled state. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: Your organization has configured multiple continuous exports to Pub/Sub for Security Command Center findings, but you discover that some critical findings are not being delivered to the Pub/Sub topic. You have verified that the NotificationConfig filter is correct and the Pub/Sub topic exists. What should you investigate to resolve this issue?
column3: Confirm that VPC Service Controls ingress rules allow the Security Command Center API to access the Pub/Sub topic if the topic is in a service perimeter.
column4: Check if the Pub/Sub subscription has expired due to 31 days of inactivity and recreate it with the 'never' expiration setting.
column5: Verify that the NotificationConfig was created with the v2 API and recreate it if it shows the 'Legacy' label in the console.
column6: Verify that the Security Command Center service agent has the securitycenter.notificationServiceAgent role on the Pub/Sub topic.
column8: When a NotificationConfig is created, a service account is automatically created and requires the securitycenter.notificationServiceAgent role to publish notifications to the Pub/Sub topic. If this role is missing, notifications will fail to be delivered. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-notifications

column2: Detection engineering"You are managing Security Command Center for a large enterprise. Security Health Analytics is generating findings for a specific set of Cloud Storage buckets that your team has determined are false positives due to a legitimate business exception. You want to prevent Security Health Analytics from creating findings for these specific buckets without affecting detection for other resources. What should you do?
column3: Disable the specific Security Health Analytics detector module that is generating the false positive findings for the entire organization.
column4: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module that excludes the specific bucket names from its detection logic.
column5: Manually set the finding state to INACTIVE for each false positive finding as they are generated.
column6: Create a dynamic mute rule with a filter that matches the specific bucket resource names to automatically mute findings for those buckets.
column8: Dynamic mute rules can target specific resources using filters that match on resource names or other attributes. The mute rule will automatically suppress findings for the specified buckets while allowing detection to continue for all other resources. Muted findings remain available for audit purposes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-mute-findings

column2: Your organization uses both Security Command Center (SCC) Premium and Google Security Operations (SecOps). You want to enhance threat hunting by correlating SCC Event Threat Detection findings with additional log sources such as Cloud Audit Logs and BigQuery context data. What should you configure in Google SecOps?
column3: Export SCC findings to Cloud Logging and create custom SQL queries in Log Analytics to correlate with other logs.
column4: Enable the CDIR SCC Enhanced rule sets to correlate Security Command Center findings with other Google Cloud data sources.
column5: Configure Event Threat Detection custom modules to directly query BigQuery tables during log analysis.
column6: Enable Applied Threat Intelligence to automatically correlate SCC findings with Mandiant IOCs.
column8: CDIR SCC Enhanced rule sets contain context-aware rules that correlate Security Command Center findings (such as Exfiltration, Defense Evasion, and Malware findings) with data from other Google Cloud sources including Cloud Audit Logs. These rule sets are specifically designed for enhanced threat detection through correlation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/cloud-threats-category

column2: Your organization has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM and wants to detect communication with known malicious IP addresses based on threat intelligence from the Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) feature. You need to ensure that only high-confidence IOCs generate alerts while reducing noise from lower-confidence indicators. What should you do?
column3: Enable only the Medium Priority Host Indicators rule set and configure custom alert thresholds in Cloud Monitoring.
column4: Create a custom YARA-L rule that matches all IP addresses against a manually maintained reference list of known malicious IPs updated weekly.
column5: Enable the Applied Threat Intelligence curated detection rule sets for Active Breach Priority Network Indicators and High Priority Network Indicators with alerting turned on.
column6: Configure all IOC feeds to generate alerts regardless of confidence score and use SOAR playbooks to filter low-confidence alerts.
column8: Applied Threat Intelligence curated detection rule sets automatically correlate ingested UDM events against Mandiant threat intelligence data and prioritize IOCs with 'Active Breach' or 'High' labels. These rule sets generate alerts only when matches meet high-confidence thresholds, reducing noise from lower-priority indicators. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-curated-detections

column2: Your organization has activated Security Command Center Premium at the organization level and needs to generate a comprehensive inventory of all Google Cloud assets with their associated IAM policy bindings for security analysis. You want to export this information to BigQuery for advanced SQL querying. Which approach should you use?
column3: Export assets from Cloud Asset Inventory using the IAM_POLICY content type to include IAM bindings for each resource alongside the asset metadata.
column4: Export assets from Cloud Asset Inventory using the RESOURCE content type and enable the 'enrichIamPolicy' flag in the export configuration.
column5: Query assets directly in Security Command Center Premium using the built-in asset query feature with IAM policy enrichment.
column6: Export assets using the Security Command Center Assets API with the includeIamBindings parameter set to true.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory's IAM_POLICY content type includes the IAM bindings on each resource. This allows you to export both asset metadata and associated IAM policies to BigQuery for comprehensive security analysis using SQL queries. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/export-bigquery

column2: You are troubleshooting Container Threat Detection findings that are missing container-level details such as the pod name and container ID. The findings only show node-level information. Your GKE clusters meet the version requirements and Container Threat Detection is enabled. What is the most likely cause of the missing container information?
column3: The REPORT_ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLES module is disabled which prevents Container Threat Detection from including container identification details.
column4: The Container Threat Detection Service Agent IAM role is missing from the service account preventing it from accessing container metadata.
column5: The Kubernetes and container runtime failed to deliver the container information in time causing the watcher DaemonSet to drop the data from the finding.
column6: The GKE cluster is running in a VPC Service Controls perimeter that blocks Container Threat Detection from accessing the Kubernetes API.
column8: Container Threat Detection passes container information through a user mode DaemonSet in a best effort manner. Container information can be dropped from the reported finding if the Kubernetes and the container runtime fail to deliver the corresponding container information in time. This is a documented limitation of the architecture. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: You are planning to enable Container Threat Detection for threat hunting across your GKE clusters. Your clusters use GKE Sandbox for some high-risk workloads. You need to ensure Container Threat Detection can monitor all workloads. What limitation must you address for Container Threat Detection deployment?
column3: Container Threat Detection requires Autopilot mode clusters and is not supported on Standard mode GKE clusters with GKE Sandbox enabled.
column4: Container Threat Detection requires installing additional security tools alongside GKE Sandbox to enable threat detection in sandboxed containers.
column5: Container Threat Detection is not compatible with GKE Sandbox, so you must disable GKE Sandbox on clusters where you want Container Threat Detection to monitor workloads.
column6: Container Threat Detection file monitoring detectors must be manually enabled for each workload running in GKE Sandbox namespaces.
column8: Container Threat Detection is not compatible with GKE Sandbox. GKE Sandbox must be disabled on GKE clusters where you want Container Threat Detection deployed. This is because GKE Sandbox provides an additional layer of kernel isolation that prevents Container Threat Detection's kernel instrumentation from functioning. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-container-threat-detection

column2: While threat hunting in Cloud Logging, you discover that an attacker may have attempted to cover their tracks by modifying logging configuration. You need to identify any API calls that could disable or modify audit log settings. Which protoPayload.methodName values should you search for in Admin Activity audit logs?
column3: google.logging.v2.LoggingServiceV2.WriteLogEntries and google.logging.v2.LoggingServiceV2.ListLogs
column4: google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink and google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink
column5: google.cloud.audit.AuditLog.Read and google.cloud.audit.AuditLog.Delete
column6: protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail and protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp
column8: These methods modify or delete log sinks, which control where logs are routed. Deleting or modifying a sink could prevent logs from reaching intended destinations, which is a common defense evasion technique. Admin Activity audit logs always record these operations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit-logging

column2: Your organization is implementing VPC Service Controls to protect BigQuery and Cloud Storage resources containing financial data. You need to test the perimeter configuration before enforcement to ensure legitimate business operations are not disrupted. You want to identify violations without blocking access. What should you do?
column3: Create the service perimeter in enforced mode and use Cloud Monitoring alerts to detect blocked requests.
column4: Create the service perimeter in dry run mode and analyze the Cloud Audit Logs to identify potential violations.
column5: Create the service perimeter with only Cloud Storage initially and add BigQuery after validating access patterns.
column6: Create the service perimeter in enforced mode and configure exception rules for all known service accounts and IP addresses.
column8: Dry run perimeters log violations as though the perimeters are enforced but don't prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to test perimeter configuration and monitor usage without blocking legitimate access. You can query logs using protoPayload.metadata.dryRun='true' to find logged violations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: Your organization wants to configure Security Command Center (SCC) to send real-time notifications to a Slack channel when critical or high-severity findings are detected. You need to set up the notification pipeline with the minimum operational overhead. What should you do?
column3: Configure a Pub/Sub topic with a continuous export filter for severity, and deploy a Cloud Run function triggered by the Pub/Sub subscription to send messages to Slack.
column4: Configure the SCC API to directly call the Slack API webhook endpoint when findings are generated using Event Threat Detection custom detectors.
column5: Enable Cloud Monitoring alerts for SCC findings and configure a notification channel to Slack using the built-in Slack integration.
column6: Configure a BigQuery streaming export with severity filters, and use a scheduled query to poll for new findings and trigger Slack notifications via Cloud Functions.
column8: SCC continuous exports to Pub/Sub allow filtering by severity and state, and Cloud Run functions can subscribe to the topic to forward notifications to Slack. This is the recommended pattern documented by Google for real-time email and chat notifications from SCC. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-enable-real-time-notifications

column2: Your organization wants to update an existing Event Threat Detection custom module to add new IP addresses from a recently published threat intelligence report. The custom module was originally created at the organization level using Terraform. What is the correct approach to update this module?
column3: Export the existing module configuration, manually edit the JSON file to add new IPs, then import it as a new version using the gcloud scc custom-modules etd import command.
column4: Update the Terraform configuration with the new IP addresses in the 'ips' array and apply the changes, which will update the existing module in place.
column5: Delete the existing custom module and create a new one with the updated IP list, as custom modules cannot be modified after creation.
column6: Create a supplementary custom module with only the new IP addresses, as each module supports a maximum of 100 IPs and the original module may have reached its limit.
column8: Event Threat Detection custom modules created with Terraform can be updated by modifying the Terraform configuration and applying the changes. The module will be updated in place with the new IP addresses. Using Terraform maintains infrastructure-as-code practices and ensures version control of your threat intelligence configurations. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: Your security team is setting up a Cloud Logging sink to export Admin Activity audit logs to BigQuery. When querying the exported data in BigQuery, the team notices that some log entries appear duplicated. You need to ensure that your security analysis queries return accurate results without duplicate entries. What should you do?
column3: Delete the existing BigQuery dataset and recreate the sink to reset the deduplication mechanism.
column4: Configure the sink to use batch mode instead of streaming mode to prevent duplicate entries during export.
column5: Enable deduplication in the BigQuery dataset settings to automatically remove duplicate entries on ingestion.
column6: Include the SELECT DISTINCT clause with the insertId and timestamp fields when querying the exported log data.
column8: Duplicate log entries can occur when there are failures in streaming log entries to BigQuery, including retries. Cloud Logging deduplicates at query time using timestamp and insertId, but BigQuery does not eliminate duplicates. Using SELECT DISTINCT on insertId and timestamp in your BigQuery queries will filter out duplicate entries. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/troubleshoot

column2: Your organization uses Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR across multiple environments representing different business units. You need to create a playbook that uses VirusTotal for enrichment and automatically selects the correct integration instance based on which environment the case originated from. What should you configure?
column3: Use environment variables in the playbook to store VirusTotal API keys and dynamically pass them to a generic integration action at runtime.
column4: Create separate playbooks for each environment and manually associate each playbook with its corresponding VirusTotal integration instance.
column5: Configure a single VirusTotal integration instance in the Default Environment and use conditional branching in the playbook to handle environment-specific logic.
column6: Configure VirusTotal integration instances for each environment, then in the playbook action select Dynamic Mode to automatically apply the correct instance at runtime.
column8: Dynamic Mode means that when the playbook runs, Google SecOps determines which environment the case came from and applies the integration instance configured for that specific environment. This is the intended approach for multi-environment deployments. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/integrations-setup/supporting-multiple-instances

column2: Your organization has Google Security Operations (SecOps) Enterprise Plus license with Applied Threat Intelligence enabled. A new threat report identifies a campaign using specific IP addresses for command and control. You want to determine if any of these IP addresses have communicated with assets in your environment over the past 90 days. What is the most effective approach to correlate these IOCs against your historical event data?
column3: Configure an IOC feed with the IP addresses and enable automatic historical matching through the IOC matches feature.
column4: Add the IP addresses to an Applied Threat Intelligence curated detection rule and wait for automatic correlation with historical events.
column5: Use the VirusTotal Search IOCs action in a SOAR playbook to query historical logs for the identified IP addresses.
column6: Create a YARA-L detection rule containing the IOCs and execute a retrohunt against historical data within the specified time range.
column8: A retrohunt lets you use a detection rule to search for matches throughout existing historical data in Google SecOps. By creating a rule with the specific IOCs and running a retrohunt, you can identify any historical communication with the threat campaign infrastructure. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Threat hunting"You are a threat hunter investigating suspicious activity in your Google Cloud environment. You need to use Cloud Logging's Log Analytics to write SQL queries that identify potential privilege escalation attempts by analyzing IAM permission changes. Which approach should you use to accomplish this task?
column3: Create a log-based metric in Cloud Logging to automatically detect IAM changes and route them to BigQuery
column4: Query Data Access audit logs using the Logging query language in Logs Explorer to search for IAM policy changes
column5: Query Admin Activity audit logs using SQL in Log Analytics to filter for IAM role binding changes and permission modifications
column6: Query Policy Denied audit logs using SQL in Log Analytics to identify successful privilege escalation attempts
column8: Admin Activity audit logs record API calls that modify the configuration or metadata of resources, including IAM permission changes. Log Analytics provides a SQL-based query interface for analyzing these logs to identify potential privilege escalation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/analyze-audit-logs

column2: You are configuring context-aware access for an IAP-protected web application deployed behind a Cloud Load Balancer. You have created access levels in Access Context Manager that restrict access to specific IP ranges and require encrypted devices. When you attempt to apply the access levels in the IAP console, they are not visible in the dropdown. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The user configuring IAP has the IAP-secured Web App User role but does not have the Access Context Manager Editor role at the project level.
column4: The access levels are defined in a project-level or folder-level access policy instead of the organizational access policy required by IAP.
column5: The access levels were created using custom access level expressions instead of basic access levels, which are not compatible with IAP.
column6: The Cloud Load Balancer backend service is not configured with the required IAP OAuth client credentials for context-aware access.
column8: IAP requires access levels to be set in the organizational access policy. The use of scoped policies (project or folder level) is not supported by IAP. Access levels must be created at the organization level to be visible when configuring IAP context-aware access. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/cloud-iap-context-aware-access-howto

column2: Your organization experienced a data breach and needs to determine the impact on sensitive data. You have previously configured Cloud DLP inspection jobs that saved findings to a BigQuery table. During the breach investigation, you need to correlate DLP findings with Cloud Logging access patterns to identify which specific sensitive data elements were potentially accessed. What should you do?
column3: Join the Cloud DLP findings table with Cloud Logging exports in BigQuery using the resource location fields from both sources to correlate sensitive data locations with access events.
column4: Query the Cloud DLP findings table in BigQuery and filter by likelihood='VERY_LIKELY' to identify only high-confidence sensitive data that may have been compromised.
column5: Create a new Cloud DLP inspection job with PublishSummaryToCscc action to send results to Security Command Center for automatic correlation with access patterns.
column6: Export both Cloud DLP findings and Cloud Logging data to separate Cloud Storage buckets and manually compare the file paths to identify overlapping resources.
column8: DLP findings stored in BigQuery include location information identifying where sensitive data resides (tables, columns, containers). By joining this with exported audit logs that show access events to those same resources, you can determine which sensitive data elements were potentially accessed during the breach. This provides precise correlation between sensitive data locations and access patterns. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/querying-findings

column2: Your security operations team is tracking the availability of a critical security API that processes threat intelligence feeds. The API returns HTTP status codes to indicate success or failure. You need to create an SLO in Cloud Monitoring to measure the percentage of successful API responses over a rolling 30-day compliance period with a 99.5% goal. Which SLI type should you configure?
column3: Request-based SLI using a TimeSeriesRatio structure that computes the ratio of 2xx responses to total responses.
column4: Windows-based SLI using a PerformanceThreshold structure that counts windows where 99.5% of requests succeeded.
column5: Windows-based SLI using a MetricRange structure that evaluates whether availability exceeds the threshold in each measurement window.
column6: Request-based SLI using a DistributionCut structure that measures the distribution of response codes across buckets.
column8: Request-based SLIs measure the ratio of good requests to total requests. TimeSeriesRatio is the appropriate structure for computing availability based on HTTP response codes. This approach counts each API call as an atomic unit of service and computes success ratio over the compliance period. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/stackdriver/docs/solutions/slo-monitoring

column2: Your organization requires that weekly Security Command Center finding reports be automatically distributed to the CISO and security leadership team. You have built a Looker Studio dashboard showing findings by severity, category, and project. You need to configure automated delivery of these reports. What should you do?
column3: Configure Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Pub/Sub message that invokes a Cloud Run service to generate and email reports.
column4: Create a Cloud Function that queries BigQuery and sends email alerts using SendGrid whenever new findings are detected.
column5: Export dashboard data to BigQuery and configure BigQuery scheduled queries to email results as CSV files.
column6: Configure a scheduled delivery in Looker Studio to send PDF reports via email to the recipients weekly.
column8: Looker Studio supports scheduled automatic report delivery that sends PDF versions of reports to specified recipients on a defined schedule. This allows stakeholders to receive regular security reports without manually accessing the dashboard. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/schedule-automatic-report-delivery

column2: Your SOC team is configuring Google Security Operations SOAR playbooks to automate enrichment workflows. You need to add VirusTotal enrichment capabilities to a playbook. Before using the VirusTotal actions in the Playbook Designer, what must you complete first?
column3: Add VirusTotal API credentials to the playbook's environment variables for the enrichment action to authenticate.
column4: Enable the VirusTotal action in the Playbook Designer by toggling it in the Actions menu settings.
column5: Download and configure the VirusTotal integration from the Content Hub.
column6: Create the VirusTotal enrichment action using the Python IDE with the Enrich Entities template.
column8: To use required actions in playbooks, you must have the integrations downloaded and configured from the Content Hub (Marketplace for SOAR only users). Each action is categorized under an integration in the system, and the integration must be installed before its actions become available in the Playbook Designer. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/using-actions-in-playbooks

column2: Your security operations team needs to create executive dashboards showing Mean Time to Respond (MTTR) and Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) trends from resolved incident data stored in Google Security Operations (SecOps). The data is exported to BigQuery and you need to visualize the metrics for stakeholder reporting. Which approach should you use?
column3: Export incident data from BigQuery to CSV files daily and import them manually into Looker Studio to build trend dashboards for executive reporting.
column4: Configure Google SecOps SOAR to generate PDF reports of incident metrics and email them directly to stakeholders on a weekly schedule.
column5: Connect Looker Studio directly to BigQuery using the native BigQuery connector, and create calculated fields to compute MTTR and MTTD from incident timestamp data.
column6: Use Cloud Monitoring to create custom dashboards that pull metrics directly from the Google SecOps SIEM without using BigQuery.
column8: Looker Studio has a native BigQuery connector that enables direct connection to BigQuery tables containing exported SecOps data. Calculated fields in Looker Studio can compute metrics like MTTR and MTTD from timestamp differences in incident data, and this approach provides interactive dashboards suitable for stakeholder reporting. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker-studio and https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/overview-chronicle-bigquery

column2: You are configuring Security Command Center Premium to prioritize security findings for resources containing sensitive customer data. Your organization uses Sensitive Data Protection discovery to classify data sensitivity levels. You want to ensure that attack path simulations account for data sensitivity when calculating risk. What should you do?
column3: Create separate Security Command Center projects for high-sensitivity and low-sensitivity resources to isolate risk calculations.
column4: Export Sensitive Data Protection findings to BigQuery and create a custom integration that updates Security Command Center security marks based on sensitivity.
column5: Configure Cloud Asset Inventory to tag resources with sensitivity labels, then use these labels in Security Command Center finding filters.
column6: Create resource value configurations and enable the option to include discovery insights from Sensitive Data Protection to automatically assign priority values based on data sensitivity.
column8: Security Command Center allows you to enable Sensitive Data Protection discovery insights within resource value configurations. When enabled, attack path simulations automatically set priority values for supported data resources based on their HIGH or MEDIUM sensitivity classifications from Sensitive Data Protection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/attack-exposure-define-high-value-resource-set

column2: Your organization experienced a critical security breach and needs to deploy an emergency patch to production GKE clusters immediately. The patched container image has not yet been attested by your CI/CD pipeline due to the urgency, but your Binary Authorization policy requires attestations. You need to deploy the image while maintaining full audit trail for compliance. What should you do?
column3: Add the emergency image path to admissionWhitelistPatterns in the Binary Authorization policy to allow deployment.
column4: Use the breakglass label in the Pod specification to override Binary Authorization enforcement and deploy the emergency image.
column5: Create a manual attestation for the image using the attestor's signing key and then deploy the image with standard procedures.
column6: Temporarily disable Binary Authorization on the cluster, deploy the image, and then re-enable Binary Authorization after deployment.
column8: Breakglass provides an emergency escape hatch that allows images to be deployed even when they violate the Binary Authorization policy. When breakglass is used, Binary Authorization logs the event to Cloud Audit Logs, maintaining a full audit trail for compliance review. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/binary-authorization/docs/using-breakglass

column2: Your organization wants to implement an automated response workflow where Cloud Functions remediate specific Security Command Center findings. After a threat finding is successfully investigated and confirmed as a false positive, the automated workflow should update the finding status. Unlike vulnerability findings that auto-resolve, threat findings require manual state management. What approach should the Cloud Function use to properly handle confirmed false positive threat findings?
column3: Delete the finding using the Security Command Center API since it has been confirmed as a false positive.
column4: Create a mute rule for the specific finding to suppress it from view while leaving the state as ACTIVE, since threat finding states remain active unless manually changed.
column5: Use the Security Command Center API to set the finding state to INACTIVE immediately after the investigation confirms it as a false positive.
column6: Wait for Event Threat Detection to automatically set the finding state to INACTIVE after detecting that the threat activity has stopped.
column8: Threat findings do not automatically change state to INACTIVE even after resolution. For confirmed false positives, Google recommends creating a mute rule rather than changing the state, as this properly handles the finding while maintaining the audit trail. The state remains ACTIVE unless explicitly changed. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/faq

column2: You are investigating a potential data exfiltration incident and need to analyze VPC Flow Logs in BigQuery to identify unusual outbound traffic patterns from internal VMs to external IP addresses. Which analytical approach should you use to identify hosts potentially involved in data exfiltration?
column3: Query for flows where the dest_port is 443 and calculate the ratio of packets_sent to packets_received to identify asymmetric HTTPS connections.
column4: Query for internal source IPs with unusually high SUM(bytes_sent) to external destinations compared to their historical baseline, grouped by destination IP ranges and time intervals.
column5: Query the reporter field for DEST values and filter for flows where the gateway object indicates DEST_GATEWAY to capture all egress traffic through Cloud Interconnect or VPN tunnels.
column6: Query for all flows with external destination IPs and create a COUNT of unique connections per source VM to identify hosts with the most external communications.
column8: Data exfiltration is characterized by internal hosts sending abnormally large amounts of data to external destinations. Comparing bytes_sent against historical baselines helps identify deviations that may indicate data theft. Grouping by destination helps identify unknown or suspicious external endpoints. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/gcp/introducing-vpc-flow-logs-network-transparency-in-near-real-time

column2: Your compliance team requires that automated security reports generated by BigQuery scheduled queries must run using a dedicated service account rather than user credentials. The scheduled queries produce daily compliance summaries that are written to a destination table. You need to configure the scheduled queries appropriately. What should you do?
column3: Use BigQuery Data Transfer Service to create a transfer configuration with oauth credentials and enable automated data pipelines.
column4: Create a Cloud Function triggered by Cloud Scheduler that uses service account impersonation to run the BigQuery query.
column5: When creating the scheduled query, select a service account under Scheduled query credential to execute the query instead of using user credentials.
column6: Configure the scheduled query with user credentials and create a separate IAM binding that maps the user to a service account role.
column8: BigQuery allows you to associate a service account with scheduled queries to execute them. This ensures the queries run with consistent permissions independent of individual users and meets the requirement for using a dedicated service account. The service account must have appropriate permissions to read source data and write to the destination. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/scheduling-queries

column2: Your organization wants to classify Cloud Storage buckets for sensitive data to support security operations. You need to configure Sensitive Data Protection discovery to generate file store data profiles that include sensitivity levels and detected infoTypes. Which configuration element determines what types of sensitive data are detected during profiling?
column3: The sensitivity calculation settings in the organization policy, which override infoType detection thresholds at the organization level.
column4: The discovery scan configuration scope settings, which define the project folders and resource types to include in profiling.
column5: The inspection template, which specifies the infoTypes that Sensitive Data Protection scans for and their associated sensitivity scores.
column6: The Cloud Storage bucket labels and metadata tags, which Sensitive Data Protection uses to infer data classification based on resource attributes.
column8: The inspection template is where you specify the infoTypes that Sensitive Data Protection looks for during profiling. The sensitivity scores of the detected infoTypes affect the resulting sensitivity level of the profiled resource. You can select from built-in infoTypes or add custom infoTypes with defined sensitivity scores. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/sensitive-data-protection/docs/data-profiles

column2: You are developing a new phishing investigation playbook in Google Security Operations SOAR that enriches URLs using third-party APIs. You want to test the playbook without impacting production cases or making unnecessary API calls to external services. What should you do?
column3: Configure the playbook actions with mock API endpoints to simulate third-party responses directly in the integration settings.
column4: Enable the Playbook Simulator, create a test case from an existing alert, and pin results for actions that call third-party APIs.
column5: Create a duplicate playbook in a separate environment and run it with live alerts to validate the workflow before deployment.
column6: Disable the playbook trigger and run the playbook manually against production cases to verify its behavior.
column8: The Playbook Simulator lets you work in a pre-production environment to test actions and observe results without impacting live production data when the playbook is deactivated. You can pin results to prevent steps from running repeatedly against third-party APIs during subsequent tests, saving time and avoiding unnecessary external calls. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-simulator

column2: During an active security incident, your incident response playbook requires immediate action when a service account is suspected to be compromised. The service account has been used to access sensitive data in Cloud Storage. Your forensic investigation team needs to preserve evidence of the malicious activity while preventing further unauthorized access. The playbook must minimize operational impact to legitimate workloads that depend on the service account. What should you do first?
column3: Disable the compromised service account key and capture Cloud Audit Logs data access records before creating a new key for legitimate workloads.
column4: Disable the service account entirely and delete all associated keys to completely prevent any further access to cloud resources.
column5: Delete the service account and rotate all credentials in the affected project immediately to ensure complete revocation of access.
column6: Remove all IAM bindings from the service account and wait 24 hours before re-enabling access for legitimate workloads.
column8: Disabling the service account key immediately prevents further unauthorized access while preserving the service account itself. Capturing data access logs preserves evidence of the malicious activity. Creating a new key allows legitimate workloads to resume operations with a clean credential. This approach minimizes operational impact while addressing the security concern. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-disable-enable

column2: Your security team is building a custom dashboard in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM to visualize IoC matches. They need to create a visualization that shows the count of IoC values over time by IoC type using a column chart. When creating the visualization tile, which combination of field types should you select from the IOC Matches Explore?
column3: Select Ioc Value and Feed Name as Filter-only fields, then configure a table calculation for count aggregation.
column4: Select Ioc Type and Event Timestamp Date as Dimensions, and Count as the Measure, then choose Column as the visualization type.
column5: Create custom fields using Looker expressions for IoC counts, then map them to a line chart visualization type.
column6: Configure dashboard-wide filters for IoC type and time range, then use the Entity Graph Explore for the visualization.
column8: When creating a chart visualization, you need to select Dimensions (attributes that describe data, like Ioc Type and Event Timestamp Date) and Measures (numeric representations like Count). For a column chart showing IoC matches over time by type, selecting these dimensions and the Count measure provides the correct data structure. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/reports/create-chart-visualization

column2: You are configuring Event Threat Detection custom modules for your organization's Security Command Center Premium deployment. Your security policy requires that findings for connections to known malicious IP addresses from your internal threat feed be classified as HIGH severity and include specific remediation instructions. How should you configure the custom module JSON template?
column3: Create the module with default settings and then use the SCC API to update the finding severity and add remediation notes after findings are generated.
column4: Configure severity and remediation through the Security Command Center console after the custom module is created, as these cannot be set in the JSON template.
column5: Set the 'finding_severity' field to 'HIGH' and include a 'remediation_steps' array with the specific instructions in the detection_parameters section.
column6: Include a 'metadata' section with 'severity' set to 'HIGH', 'description' with threat details, and 'recommendation' with remediation instructions, along with the 'ips' array.
column8: The Event Threat Detection custom module JSON template uses the metadata section to define severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), description text, and recommendation text for remediation guidance. This configuration ensures findings are generated with the specified severity and help security teams understand how to respond. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: "Your organization runs critical CI/CD workloads on GKE that involve significant file I/O operations. You want to enable Container Threat Detection file monitoring detectors to detect access or modification to critical system files. However, you are concerned about potential performance impact. What should you do?
column3: Enable file monitoring detectors in a test environment first, evaluate the performance impact on workloads with significant file I/O, and then deploy to production.
column4: Enable all Container Threat Detection detectors including file monitoring on production immediately, as they have minimal performance overhead.
column5: Disable Container Threat Detection entirely on CI/CD clusters to avoid any performance impact on file operations.
column6: Configure Container Threat Detection to only scan containers during non-business hours to minimize performance impact.
column8: Container Threat Detection file monitoring detectors that monitor file operations can potentially cause performance degradation for workloads with significant file I/O. Google recommends evaluating the impact on any workload before enabling these detectors in production. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your organization uses Security Health Analytics in Security Command Center Premium tier. You need to create a custom detection rule that generates findings when Cloud KMS CryptoKeys have a rotation period exceeding 90 days. What should you do?
column3: Configure a Cloud Asset Inventory feed to export CryptoKey metadata to Pub/Sub and create a Cloud Function that generates SCC findings when rotation periods exceed 90 days.
column4: Create a Security Health Analytics custom module with a YAML definition that includes a CEL expression evaluating the resource.rotationPeriod property against duration('7776000s').
column5: Create an Event Threat Detection custom module using a JSON template to monitor Cloud KMS API calls and detect keys with long rotation periods in Cloud Audit Logs.
column6: Modify the built-in KMS_KEY_NOT_ROTATED detector by updating its threshold parameter to 90 days through the Security Command Center management API.
column8: Security Health Analytics custom modules use YAML definitions with CEL expressions to evaluate resource properties. The rotationPeriod property can be compared against a duration value (90 days = 7,776,000 seconds) using standard CEL operators. The module must specify cloudkms.googleapis.com/CryptoKey as the resource type. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/custom-modules-sha-code

column2: Incident response"Your security operations team wants to detect multi-stage attack patterns where an attacker first performs credential theft and then escalates privileges within a 30-minute window. You need to implement this detection in Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM using YARA-L. Which rule design approach should you use?
column3: Create a YARA-L rule using the metrics function to count credential theft and privilege escalation events per user and alert when both exceed threshold values.
column4: Create a multi-event YARA-L rule with a match section correlating events by principal.user.userid over a 30-minute window, and use the condition section to require both event types.
column5: Use a single-event YARA-L rule with the outcome section to track timestamps and calculate time differences between credential theft and privilege escalation events.
column6: Create two separate single-event YARA-L rules and configure an alert grouping rule to combine them when triggered within 30 minutes of each other.
column8: Multi-event YARA-L rules allow correlation across multiple event types within a defined time window. By correlating on principal.user.userid, the rule can detect when the same user is involved in both credential theft and privilege escalation events within the 30-minute period. The match section specifies the correlation field and time window. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-2-0-overview

column2: Your security team has identified that several service accounts in your Google Cloud environment have permissions to impersonate service accounts in other projects. You want to systematically identify and address these lateral movement risks. Which approach should you use?
column3: Configure VPC Service Controls perimeters around each project to prevent service accounts from accessing resources in other projects and eliminate cross-project impersonation.
column4: Create custom IAM roles for all service accounts that exclude iam.serviceAccounts.actAs and iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken permissions to prevent any form of service account impersonation across the organization.
column5: Use Cloud Audit Logs to search for all iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken permission grants across your organization and immediately revoke any cross-project grants to prevent lateral movement.
column6: Review lateral movement insights in IAM Recommender, which identifies roles allowing service accounts in one project to impersonate service accounts in another project, and prioritize recommendations that reduce impersonation permissions not used in the last 90 days.
column8: IAM Recommender generates lateral movement insights that identify roles allowing service accounts to impersonate other service accounts across projects. The insights show whether impersonation permissions have been used in the last 90 days, helping you safely identify and remove unnecessary permissions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/lateral-movement-insights

column2: Your security team has received new threat intelligence indicating that a specific threat actor group is using previously unknown malware hashes. You need to determine whether any of these newly discovered indicators of compromise (IOCs) have been observed in your organization's historical security telemetry during the past 6 months. You are using Google Security Operations (SecOps). What should you do?
column3: Export 6 months of raw logs to BigQuery and run SQL queries to search for the malware hashes manually.
column4: Create a YARA-L rule containing the new malware hashes and execute a retrohunt against the historical data for the past 6 months.
column5: Use the IOC matches page to manually filter and search for the hashes, which will automatically scan all historical data.
column6: Submit the IOCs to Security Command Center's Event Threat Detection and wait for alerts to be generated on historical data.
column8: Retrohunts enable you to use a rule to search for detections throughout existing data in Google SecOps. With 12 months of hot data retention by default, you can effectively search for newly discovered IOCs across 6 months of historical logs by running the rule against historical data. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization is deploying Google Security Operations (SecOps) SOAR to automate threat response across both cloud infrastructure and an on-premises data center that cannot be accessed directly from the cloud. The playbooks need to execute endpoint isolation actions against systems in the on-premises environment. What should you configure to enable this capability?
column3: Create custom Python scripts in the IDE that establish SSH connections to on-premises systems and execute isolation commands directly.
column4: Configure a VPN connection between Google SecOps and the on-premises network, then use standard cloud integrations to reach on-premises endpoints.
column5: Install the EDR integration on a cloud-hosted proxy server that forwards commands to on-premises endpoints through firewall rules.
column6: Deploy a Remote Agent in the on-premises environment, configure the integration to run remotely, and use the integration actions within your playbooks.
column8: The Remote Agent securely connects a cloud Google SecOps instance to remote sites, enabling execution of actions and playbooks on remote environments. The agent pulls tasks from Google SecOps, executes them on the remote network, and returns results. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/working-with-remote-agents/what-is-a-remote-agent

column2: Your organization has enabled Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) curated detections in Google SecOps Enterprise Plus. After reviewing alert volumes, you notice that Medium priority ATI alerts are generating significant noise and want to focus analyst attention on the most critical threats. You need to configure the ATI detection rule packs to reduce alert fatigue while maintaining detection of high-risk indicators. What should you do?
column3: Modify the GTI score threshold in SIEM Settings to only ingest IOCs with scores above 90, which automatically filters out Medium priority indicators before they generate alerts.
column4: Disable the ATI Medium priority rule pack entirely and configure a scheduled retrohunt to periodically scan for Medium priority IOC matches on a weekly basis.
column5: Create custom YARA-L rules that filter ATI detections by adding a condition in the outcome section that excludes alerts where the priority equals Medium.
column6: In the Curated Detections settings, keep ATI Medium priority rule packs in non-alerting mode while enabling alerting for Active Breach and High priority rule packs.
column8: Google recommends keeping ATI Medium priority rule packs in non-alerting mode due to the potential volume of Medium priority indicators. Active Breach and High priority alerts are based on higher-confidence intelligence features like Active IR status, GTI verdict, and attribution, making them more actionable. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: Your security team is using Google Security Operations (SecOps) with Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) enabled. You notice that the IOC matches page shows indicators with different priority levels. You want to understand which indicators require immediate investigation because they were observed in active Mandiant incident response investigations. Which priority level should you filter for to identify these high-confidence, breach-associated IOCs?
column3: Filter for IOCs with an IC-Score above 95, which indicates direct correlation with Mandiant active investigations.
column4: Filter for IOCs with Critical severity, which represents the highest tier of Mandiant-validated threat indicators.
column5: Filter for IOCs with the Active Breach priority level, which indicates indicators observed in Mandiant investigations associated with active or past compromises.
column6: Filter for IOCs with the High priority level, which indicates all indicators directly observed during Mandiant incident response engagements.
column8: The Active breach model prioritizes indicators that Mandiant observed in active or past compromises, where the GTI Verdict is Malicious and GTI Severity is High. These are the highest confidence IOCs requiring immediate attention. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-prioritization

column2: Your security team maintains a list of 500 IP addresses associated with known command-and-control infrastructure. You want to create a detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) that generates alerts when network traffic involves any of these IP addresses. Which approach should you use?
column3: Write a YARA-L rule with 500 individual conditions using OR operators to match each IP address.
column4: Create a reference list containing the IP addresses and use the 'in' operator in a YARA-L rule to match against the list.
column5: Create a CIDR reference list and add each IP address as a /32 subnet for matching.
column6: Upload the IP addresses as a custom threat intelligence feed and enable Applied Threat Intelligence.
column8: Reference lists are designed for this use case, allowing you to maintain a list of values that can be efficiently matched against in YARA-L rules using the 'in' operator. The syntax $e.target.ip in %reference_list_name enables detection across all listed IPs without hardcoding values. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-best-practices

column2: You are configuring alerting policies in Cloud Monitoring for your organization's security service endpoints. The security team requires that alerts only trigger after sustained failures to reduce false positives from brief network issues. An alert should fire only when uptime checks fail continuously for at least 5 minutes across multiple checker regions. What should you configure?
column3: Configure the notification channel with a 5-minute delay before sending notifications and set the alerting policy trigger count to 5 consecutive failures.
column4: Create a log-based alerting policy that monitors Cloud Logging for uptime check failure entries and uses a counter threshold of 5 failures before triggering.
column5: Configure the alerting policy with a retest window (duration) of 300 seconds (5 minutes) and use an aggregation that requires failures from multiple time series across different checker regions.
column6: Configure the alerting policy with no retest window and set the check frequency of the uptime check to 5 minutes to space out checks and reduce false positives.
column8: The retest window (duration field) specifies how long the threshold must be violated before an incident is created. Setting it to 300 seconds ensures the condition must be met for 5 continuous minutes. Aggregating across checker regions prevents single-region issues from triggering alerts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/concepts-indepth

column2: Your organization requires all security audit logs to be retained in Cloud Storage for 7 years to meet regulatory compliance requirements. You need to ensure that logs cannot be deleted before the retention period expires and that logs are automatically deleted after 7 years to minimize storage costs. What should you configure on the Cloud Storage bucket?
column3: Configure a retention policy with a 7-year retention period and lock it, then configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to delete objects older than 7 years.
column4: Configure Object Lifecycle Management with a delete action at 7 years and enable Bucket Lock to prevent policy modification.
column5: Configure a retention policy with a 7-year retention period without locking it, which will prevent deletion and automatically remove objects after 7 years.
column6: Configure an Object Lifecycle Management rule to delete objects older than 7 years and enable Object Versioning to prevent accidental deletion.
column8: A locked retention policy prevents deletion of objects before the retention period expires, meeting compliance requirements. The Object Lifecycle Management rule automatically deletes objects after they meet the age condition, reducing storage costs. These two features work together for compliance and cost optimization. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock and https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/lifecycle
